claims.label: Animal parts are either uniform (homogeneous) or composite
claims.claim: The parts of animals are of two kinds: simple parts, which divide into parts like themselves (as flesh into flesh), and composite parts, which do not (a hand does not divide into hands).
claims.quote: Of the parts of animals some are simple: to wit, all such as divide into parts uniform with themselves, as flesh into flesh; others are composite, such as divide into parts not uniform with themselves
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Parts of different genera can correspond only by analogy, as feather to scale
claims.claim: Animals of different genera may have parts that are the same only by analogy: bone corresponds to fish-bone, nail to hoof, hand to claw, and the feather of a bird to the scale of a fish.
claims.quote: they are the same only in the way of analogy, as, for instance, bone is only analogous to fish-bone, nail to hoof, hand to claw, and scale to feather; for what the feather is in a bird, the scale is in a fish.
claims.scope: Animals of different genera, e.g. birds and fishes
measurable_quantities: correspondence of integumentary and skeletal structures across taxa
claims.candidate_data: Anatomy ontologies such as Uberon and the Phenoscape Knowledgebase, which record homology and analogy relations between structures.

claims.label: The gadfly develops from river worms that leave the water
claims.claim: Some animals live first in water and later change their shape and live out of water; the gadfly develops from river worms in this way.
claims.quote: Some animals at first live in water, and by and by change their shape and live out of water, as is the case with river worms, for out of these the gadfly develops.
claims.scope: Insects with aquatic larvae; the 'gadfly' (oistros, an insect of uncertain identity)
measurable_quantities: larval habitat (aquatic vs terrestrial) of the species identified as the gadfly
occurrence of metamorphosis from aquatic larva to aerial adult
claims.candidate_data: Insect life-history and larval-habitat records such as the freshwater ecology trait databases and the Animal Diversity Web.

claims.label: No bird with crooked talons is gregarious
claims.claim: No bird with crooked talons (a bird of prey) lives in flocks.
claims.quote: no bird furnished with crooked talons is gregarious
claims.scope: Birds with hooked talons (raptors: eagles, hawks, falcons, owls, vultures)
measurable_quantities: flocking or colonial behaviour across raptor species
claims.candidate_data: AVONET and the Birds of the World species accounts for social and flocking behaviour; EltonTraits for diet to define raptors.

claims.label: Every domesticated kind of animal also exists in a wild form
claims.claim: Whenever a kind of animal is found domesticated, the same kind is always also found wild, as with horses, cattle, swine, sheep, goats and dogs.
claims.quote: whenever a race of animals is found domesticated, the same is always to be found in a wild condition; as we find to be the case with horses, kine, swine, (men), sheep, goats, and dogs.
claims.scope: Domesticated animals: horse, cattle, pig, sheep, goat, dog (and, in the translator's bracket, man)
measurable_quantities: existence of extant wild or feral populations for each domesticated species
claims.candidate_data: IUCN Red List status of wild progenitors and GBIF occurrence records of wild and feral populations of domestic species.

claims.label: An animal with a bladder always has an intestine, but not conversely
claims.claim: Every animal that has a bladder for wet residue also has an intestine for dry residue, but an animal may have an intestine without a bladder.
claims.quote: In other words, an animal has a bowel or intestine if it have a bladder; but an animal may have a bowel and be without a bladder.
claims.scope: All animals with organs for excreting residue
measurable_quantities: presence of a urinary bladder
presence of an intestine
claims.candidate_data: Comparative anatomy compiled in Uberon and the Phenoscape Knowledgebase for presence/absence of urinary bladder and intestine across taxa.

claims.label: Touch is the only sense common to all animals
claims.claim: Touch is the one and only sense that all animals possess.
claims.quote: One sense, and one alone, is common to all animals-the sense of touch.
measurable_quantities: presence of mechanosensory capacity across animal phyla
presence of other senses (vision, chemoreception, hearing) across phyla
claims.candidate_data: Comparative sensory biology literature and Animal Diversity Web phylum accounts; no single dataset known.

claims.label: Animals with more than four feet are bloodless
claims.claim: All animals with more than four feet are bloodless, as are the bee, the wasp, the cuttlefish and the crawfish, while animals with blood have no feet, two feet or four feet.
claims.quote: other animals are bloodless, such as the bee and the wasp, and, of marine animals, the cuttle-fish, the crawfish, and all such animals as have more than four feet.
claims.scope: All footed animals; 'bloodless' roughly the invertebrates, 'blooded' roughly the vertebrates
measurable_quantities: number of legs
presence of red blood (vertebrate-type blood)
claims.candidate_data: Open Tree of Life for vertebrate/invertebrate membership and Phenoscape or Uberon for limb counts.

claims.label: In an egg the embryo forms from part of it, the rest being food
claims.claim: In an egg the embryo arises from only part of the egg, and the rest serves as food for the developing embryo, whereas a grub develops into the animal as a whole.
claims.quote: in respect to its primitive germ it comes from part only of the egg, while the rest serves for food as the germ develops.
claims.scope: Oviparous animals (eggs) contrasted with grub-bearing animals (insects)
measurable_quantities: fraction of egg contents incorporated into embryo vs consumed as yolk
claims.candidate_data: Developmental biology literature on yolk use in bird and reptile eggs; no single dataset known.

claims.label: Sharks hatch eggs inside their own bodies
claims.claim: Some viviparous animals, such as the sharks, hatch eggs inside their own bodies, while others, such as man and the horse, carry a live foetus.
claims.quote: Of viviparous animals, some hatch eggs in their own interior, as creatures of the shark kind; others engender in their interior a live foetus, as man and the horse.
claims.scope: Selachians (cartilaginous fishes) of the shark kind; viviparous mammals
measurable_quantities: reproductive mode (oviparity, yolk-sac viviparity/ovoviviparity, placental viviparity) across shark species
claims.candidate_data: FishBase reproductive-guild fields and published compilations of chondrichthyan reproductive modes.

claims.label: Bloodless animals are largest in mild climates and in the sea
claims.claim: Among bloodless animals, the largest kinds live in milder climates, and those living in the sea are larger than those living on land or in fresh water.
claims.quote: And of these bloodless genera, those are the largest that dwell in milder climates, and those that inhabit the sea are larger than those living on dry land or in fresh water.
measurable_quantities: maximum body size of invertebrate taxa by latitude/climate
maximum body size by habitat (marine, terrestrial, freshwater)
claims.candidate_data: SeaLifeBase body sizes for marine invertebrates, GBIF occurrences for climate of range, and published invertebrate body-size compilations.

claims.label: All hair-coated animals are viviparous
claims.claim: Every animal with a coat of hair (counting the spines of hedgehogs and porcupines as hair) bears live young.
claims.quote: All animals, however, that are hair-coated are viviparous.
measurable_quantities: reproductive mode across hair-bearing species, including monotremes
claims.candidate_data: The Amniote Life-History Database and AnAge for reproductive mode across mammals.

claims.label: Women's skulls have one circular suture, men's usually three meeting
claims.claim: The skull of a woman has one circular suture, while the skull of a man, as a general rule, has three sutures meeting at a point.
claims.quote: The skull has sutures: one, of circular form, in the case of women; in the case of men, as a general rule, three meeting at a point.
measurable_quantities: number and configuration of cranial sutures in male and female skulls
claims.candidate_data: Human cranial CT and osteological collections such as those shared on MorphoSource.

claims.label: The mole has stunted eyes hidden under the skin
claims.claim: The mole cannot see and has no externally visible eyes, but beneath its skin lie the eye region and the dark parts of the eyes, stunted and overgrown by skin; it is the only viviparous animal without eyes.
claims.quote: For in point of absolute fact it cannot see, and has no eyes visible externally; but when the outer skin is removed, it is found to have the place where eyes are usually situated, and the black parts of the eyes rightly situated
claims.scope: The mole (Mediterranean moles, Talpa, or possibly mole-rats, Spalax)
measurable_quantities: presence and size of eyes beneath the skin
light perception or visual function
claims.candidate_data: Specimen CT scans on MorphoSource and anatomical studies of eye reduction in Talpa and Spalax.

claims.label: Man is the only, or nearly only, animal with varied eye colours
claims.claim: Man is the only, or nearly the only, animal whose eyes vary in colour between individuals; other animals as a rule have eyes of a single colour, though some horses have blue eyes.
claims.quote: Man is the only, or nearly the only, creature, that has eyes of diverse colours. Animals, as a rule, have eyes of one colour only.
claims.scope: Man compared with other animals; horses as an exception
measurable_quantities: within-species variation in iris colour across species
claims.candidate_data: Comparative iris-colour surveys of mammals and birds in the literature; no single dataset known.

claims.label: The inner ear connects to the palate, not to the brain
claims.claim: The inner cavity of the ear has no passage to the brain but does have a passage to the palate.
claims.quote: This receptacle does not communicate by any passage with the brain, but does so with the palate
measurable_quantities: presence of a canal from middle ear to pharynx (auditory tube)
presence of an open passage from ear to brain cavity
claims.candidate_data: Human and comparative anatomy in Uberon and the Foundational Model of Anatomy.

claims.label: Man is the only animal with ears that cannot move them
claims.claim: Of all animals that have ears, man is the only one that cannot move them.
claims.quote: Of animals possessed of ears man is the only one that cannot move this organ.
measurable_quantities: capacity for voluntary pinna movement across mammal species, including apes
claims.candidate_data: Comparative studies of auricular musculature in primates and other mammals; no single dataset known.

claims.label: The crocodile alone moves its upper jaw instead of its lower
claims.claim: All animals move the lower jaw except the river crocodile, which moves only its upper jaw.
claims.quote: All animals move the lower jaw, with the exception of the river crocodile; this creature moves the upper jaw only.
claims.scope: Animals with jaws; the Nile crocodile
measurable_quantities: relative motion of upper jaw (skull) and lower jaw during jaw opening in crocodiles
claims.candidate_data: Published biomechanics and video kinematics of crocodylian feeding; no single dataset known.

claims.label: Man has eight ribs on each side
claims.claim: The human trunk has eight ribs on each side.
claims.quote: Common to the upper and lower part of the trunk are the 'ribs', eight on either side
measurable_quantities: number of ribs per side in humans
claims.candidate_data: Standard human anatomy and skeletal datasets, e.g. the Foundational Model of Anatomy and human CT collections on MorphoSource.

claims.label: Man has the largest and moistest brain for his size
claims.claim: Relative to body size, man has the largest and the moistest brain of any animal.
claims.quote: But, taking size for size of animal, the largest brain, and the moistest, is that of man.
claims.scope: Man compared with all other animals that have a brain
measurable_quantities: brain mass relative to body mass across species
brain water content
claims.candidate_data: Comparative brain- and body-mass compilations for mammals and birds, and AnAge for body mass.

claims.label: The brain is bloodless, has no veins and is cold
claims.claim: In all animals the brain is bloodless, has no veins in it and is naturally cold to the touch.
claims.quote: The brain in all animals is bloodless, devoid of veins, and naturally cold to the touch
measurable_quantities: blood perfusion and vascular density of brain tissue
brain temperature relative to body
claims.candidate_data: Cerebral blood-flow and brain-temperature measurements in the physiology literature; Allen Brain Atlas vasculature data.

claims.label: The heart has three cavities, the right largest and the left smallest
claims.claim: The heart has three cavities: the right-hand one is the largest, the left-hand one the smallest, and the middle one intermediate in size.
claims.quote: It has three cavities, as has been said: the right-hand one the largest of the three, the left-hand one the least, and the middle one intermediate in size.
claims.scope: Man and the larger blooded animals
measurable_quantities: number of heart chambers
relative chamber volumes
claims.candidate_data: Comparative cardiac anatomy in Uberon and human cardiac imaging data.

claims.label: The lung is the organ most richly supplied with blood
claims.claim: In animals that have a lung and bear live young, the lung is the organ most richly supplied with blood, being spongy and reached at every pore by branches of the great vein; it is not empty, as some suppose.
claims.quote: the lung is of all organs the most richly supplied with blood; for the lung is throughout spongy in texture, and along by every single pore in it go branches from the great vein.
claims.scope: Animals with lungs that are viviparous (mammals)
measurable_quantities: blood volume or blood flow per gram of tissue by organ
claims.candidate_data: Organ blood-flow and blood-volume tables in mammalian physiology references.

claims.label: The right kidney lies higher than the left in all animals
claims.claim: In all animals that have kidneys, the right kidney lies higher in the body than the left.
claims.quote: In all animals that are provided with this organ, the right kidney is situated higher up than the other.
measurable_quantities: relative craniocaudal position of right and left kidneys across species
claims.candidate_data: Veterinary and human anatomical imaging; comparative anatomy references.

claims.label: The lion's neck is a single bone without vertebrae
claims.claim: The lion's neck consists of a single bone instead of vertebrae.
claims.quote: The lion has its neck composed of one single bone instead of vertebrae
measurable_quantities: number of separate cervical vertebrae in the lion
claims.candidate_data: Lion skeletal specimens and CT scans on MorphoSource; mammalian cervical vertebra counts in the literature.

claims.label: The elephant sleeps lying on its side, not standing
claims.claim: The elephant does not sleep standing; it bends its legs, settles down and sleeps lying on one side.
claims.quote: The elephant does not sleep standing, as some were wont to assert, but it bends its legs and settles down
measurable_quantities: sleep posture (standing vs recumbent) in elephants
claims.candidate_data: Published actigraphy and video studies of elephant sleep in the wild and in zoos.

claims.label: Horned animals are mostly cloven-hoofed; none is solid-hoofed with two horns
claims.claim: The great majority of horned animals are cloven-hoofed, and no solid-hoofed animal with a pair of horns has ever been found.
claims.quote: The great majority of the horned animals are cloven-footed, as the ox, the stag, the goat; and a solid-hooved animal with a pair of horns has never yet been met with.
measurable_quantities: co-occurrence of paired horns or antlers with hoof type across ungulates
claims.candidate_data: Phenoscape and PanTHERIA-style trait compilations of ungulate headgear and digit number; Open Tree of Life for taxon coverage.

claims.label: Only the deer sheds its horns, annually after age two
claims.claim: The deer is the only animal that sheds its horns; it does so every year after reaching the age of two and grows them again.
claims.quote: The deer is the only animal that sheds its horns, and it does so annually, after reaching the age of two years, and again renews them.
claims.scope: Deer and all other horned animals
measurable_quantities: annual shedding of headgear by species
age at first antler cast
claims.candidate_data: Comparative literature on antler cycles in cervids and horn-sheath shedding in pronghorn; Animal Diversity Web accounts.

claims.label: The fox, wolf, marten and weasel have a bony penis
claims.claim: In some animals the penis is bony, as in the fox, the wolf, the marten and the weasel.
claims.quote: in other cases it is bony, as with the fox, the wolf, the marten, and the weasel; for this organ in the weasel has a bone.
measurable_quantities: presence of a baculum (os penis)
claims.candidate_data: Published comparative datasets on baculum presence across mammals; museum specimens on MorphoSource.

claims.label: No animal has both tusks and horns, nor does any saw-toothed animal
claims.claim: No animal has both tusks and horns, and no animal with interlocking pointed (saw-like) teeth has either tusks or horns.
claims.quote: No animal is there that possesses both tusks and horns, nor yet do either of these structures exist in any animal possessed of 'saw-teeth'.
measurable_quantities: co-occurrence of tusks and horns/antlers across species
co-occurrence of carnassial or interlocking dentition with tusks or horns
claims.candidate_data: Mammal trait compilations (PanTHERIA, Phenoscape) for headgear and dentition; Animal Diversity Web species accounts.

claims.label: No animal sheds its molars, and the pig sheds no teeth at all
claims.claim: Man sheds his front teeth, but no animal sheds its molars, and the pig sheds none of its teeth at all.
claims.quote: And man sheds his front teeth; but there is no instance of an animal that sheds its molars. The pig sheds none of its teeth at all.
claims.scope: Man and mammals with tooth replacement; the pig
measurable_quantities: replacement of deciduous cheek teeth by species
presence of tooth replacement in pigs
claims.candidate_data: Mammalian dental eruption and replacement schedules in veterinary and comparative odontology references.

claims.label: Teeth blacken with age except in the horse, whose teeth whiten
claims.claim: As animals grow older their teeth generally become blacker, but the horse's teeth become whiter with age.
claims.quote: for, generally speaking, as animals grow older their teeth get blacker, but the horse's teeth grow whiter with age.
measurable_quantities: tooth colour by age in horses and other mammals
claims.candidate_data: Equine dental ageing guides and photographic datasets of tooth wear by age.

claims.label: Males have more teeth than females in man, sheep, goats and swine
claims.claim: In men, sheep, goats and swine, males have more teeth than females.
claims.quote: Males have more teeth than females in the case of men, sheep, goats, and swine
measurable_quantities: adult tooth count by sex
claims.candidate_data: Dental formulae in mammal anatomy references and the Animal Diversity Web; sex-specific dental records in veterinary literature.

claims.label: Animals with more teeth live longer, as a rule
claims.claim: As a rule, animals with more teeth live longer, and those with fewer and more thinly set teeth are correspondingly short-lived.
claims.quote: the more teeth they have the more long-lived are they, as a rule, while those are short-lived in proportion that have teeth fewer in number and thinly set.
claims.scope: Animals with teeth (men, sheep, goats, swine and others)
measurable_quantities: tooth count
maximum or mean lifespan
claims.candidate_data: AnAge for maximum lifespan combined with dental formulae from mammal anatomy references; human longevity cohorts with dental counts.

claims.label: Oviparous quadrupeds lack external ears, breasts and a copulatory organ
claims.claim: Oviparous blooded quadrupeds have no external ears but only an auditory passage, no breasts, no copulatory organ, and no external testicles, only internal ones.
claims.quote: Again, oviparous blooded quadrupeds are unprovided with ears, but possess only the passage for hearing; neither have they breasts, nor a copulatory organ, nor external testicles, but internal ones only
measurable_quantities: presence of external ear
presence of mammary glands
presence of intromittent organ (hemipenes, phallus)
testis position
claims.candidate_data: Comparative reptile and amphibian anatomy in Phenoscape and Uberon; herpetological anatomy literature.

claims.label: River crocodiles spend the day on land and the night in water
claims.claim: As a rule, river crocodiles spend the daytime on land and the night in the water.
claims.quote: As a rule, they pass the day-time on land and the nighttime in the water
measurable_quantities: proportion of time on land vs in water by time of day
claims.candidate_data: Telemetry and temperature-logger studies of Nile crocodile thermoregulation; Movebank tracking data where available.

claims.label: Crocodiles enter water at night because it is then warmer than the air
claims.claim: Crocodiles spend the night in the water because at night the water is warmer than the open air.
claims.quote: for the temperature of the water is at night-time more genial than that of the open air.
measurable_quantities: night-time water vs air temperature in crocodile habitats
crocodile body temperature by location at night
claims.candidate_data: Thermoregulation studies of crocodylians with body-temperature loggers; meteorological and water-temperature records for their habitats.

claims.label: The chameleon changes colour when it inflates itself with air
claims.claim: The chameleon changes colour when it is inflated with air, turning black, or green with black spots, over its whole body including the eyes and tail.
claims.quote: The change in its colour takes place when it is inflated with air; it is then black, not unlike the crocodile, or green like the lizard but black-spotted like the pard.
measurable_quantities: co-occurrence of body inflation and colour change
colour states displayed
claims.candidate_data: Published behavioural and physiological studies of chameleon colour change; no single dataset known.

claims.label: High-flying birds are four-toed, most three-forward one-back
claims.claim: Birds that fly high are all four-toed; most have three toes in front and one behind, and a few, such as the wryneck, have two in front and two behind.
claims.quote: Birds that fly high in air are in all cases four-toed: that is, the greater part have three toes in front and one behind in place of a heel; some few have two in front and two behind, as the wryneck.
claims.scope: Birds that fly high; the wryneck (Jynx torquilla)
measurable_quantities: toe number
toe arrangement (anisodactyl, zygodactyl)
flight habit
claims.candidate_data: AVONET morphological traits and published foot-type classifications of birds.

claims.label: No fish has a neck, limbs, testicles or breasts
claims.claim: No fish has a neck, any limb, testicles (internal or external), or breasts.
claims.quote: No fish has a neck, or any limb, or testicles at all, within or without, or breasts.
measurable_quantities: presence of neck
presence of limbs
presence of testes
presence of mammary glands
claims.candidate_data: FishBase and Phenoscape for fish anatomy, including gonad anatomy.

claims.label: The dolphin has two breasts near its genitals
claims.claim: The dolphin bears live young directly and has two breasts placed near its genitals rather than high up, with no visible teats but two slits from which milk flows.
claims.quote: Thus the dolphin is directly viviparous, and accordingly we find it furnished with two breasts, not situated high up, but in the neighbourhood of the genitals.
measurable_quantities: number and position of mammary glands and slits
claims.candidate_data: Cetacean anatomy literature and specimen records; Animal Diversity Web accounts.

claims.label: Fishes have no organs or passages for hearing or smell
claims.claim: Of the sense organs fishes have only eyes; they have neither the organs of hearing and smell nor any passages for them.
claims.quote: with regard to the organs connected with the other senses, hearing and smell, they are devoid alike of the organs themselves and of passages indicative of them.
measurable_quantities: presence of inner ear
presence of nares and olfactory epithelium
claims.candidate_data: Phenoscape and FishBase for fish sensory anatomy.

claims.label: Scaly fish lay eggs; cartilaginous fish bear live young
claims.claim: Scaly fishes are always oviparous, and cartilaginous fishes are all viviparous except the fishing-frog.
claims.quote: scaly fish are invariably oviparous, but cartilaginous fishes are all viviparous, with the single exception of the fishing-frog.
claims.scope: Scaly (bony) fishes and selachians (cartilaginous fishes); the fishing-frog (anglerfish, Lophius)
measurable_quantities: reproductive mode across scaly bony fishes and chondrichthyans
claims.candidate_data: FishBase reproductive-guild fields for teleosts and chondrichthyans.

claims.label: Some oxen and the horse have a bone inside the heart
claims.claim: In one kind of ox, though not in every individual, a bone is found inside the heart, and the horse's heart also has a bone in it.
claims.quote: there is one species of ox where, though not in all cases, a bone is found inside the heart. And, by the way, the horse's heart also has a bone inside it.
measurable_quantities: presence and prevalence of an os cordis (cardiac bone) in cattle and horses
claims.candidate_data: Veterinary anatomy literature on the os cordis in ruminants and equids.

claims.label: Deer, horse, mule, ass, seal and some pigs lack a gall-bladder
claims.claim: Among viviparous quadrupeds the deer, the roe, the horse, the mule, the ass, the seal and some kinds of pig have no gall-bladder.
claims.quote: Of viviparous quadrupeds the deer is without the organ, as also the roe, the horse, the mule, the ass, the seal, and some kinds of pigs.
claims.scope: Deer, roe deer, horse, mule, ass, seal, pigs
measurable_quantities: presence of a gall-bladder by species
claims.candidate_data: Comparative mammalian anatomy literature and Uberon/Phenoscape presence-absence records for the gall bladder.

claims.label: Stags always have about twenty maggots inside the head
claims.claim: Without exception, stags have maggots living inside the head, in the hollow beneath the root of the tongue and near the first vertebra, usually about twenty in a cluster.
claims.quote: However, without any exception, stags are found to have maggots living inside the head
measurable_quantities: prevalence of nasopharyngeal larvae in deer
number of larvae per host
claims.candidate_data: Parasitological surveys of deer nasal bot flies (Cephenemyia) and host-parasite databases.

claims.label: No fish or bird has kidneys or a bladder
claims.claim: No oviparous animal that is not a quadruped, whether fish or bird, is known to have kidneys or a bladder.
claims.quote: Of the ovipara that are not quadrupedal there is no instance known of an animal, whether fish or bird, provided with these organs.
measurable_quantities: presence of kidneys
presence of urinary bladder
claims.candidate_data: Comparative anatomy in Uberon and the Phenoscape Knowledgebase for kidney and bladder presence in fishes and birds.

claims.label: Horned animals lacking upper front teeth have four stomachs and ruminate
claims.claim: Horned quadrupeds that lack a full set of teeth in both jaws have a stomach of four chambers, and these are the animals that chew the cud.
claims.quote: such of the horned animals as are not equally furnished with teeth in both jaws are furnished with four such chambers. These animals, by the way, are those that are said to chew the cud.
measurable_quantities: presence of upper incisors
number of stomach chambers
rumination
claims.candidate_data: Comparative digestive anatomy literature and mammal trait compilations; Animal Diversity Web accounts.

claims.label: Serpents have thirty ribs, as many as the days of a month
claims.claim: Serpents have thirty ribs.
claims.quote: Their ribs are as numerous as the days of the month; in other words, they are thirty in number.
measurable_quantities: number of rib pairs in snakes
claims.candidate_data: Vertebral and rib counts for snakes in herpetological literature and CT scans on MorphoSource.

claims.label: Fishes, gilled animals and serpents have no testicles
claims.claim: No fish, no other gill-bearing animal and no serpent has testicles; nor does any footless animal except those that are viviparous within themselves.
claims.quote: No fish is furnished with testicles, nor any other creature that has gills, nor any serpent whatever: nor, in short, any animal devoid of feet, save such only as are viviparous within themselves.
claims.scope: fishes, gill-bearing animals, serpents (snakes), footless animals other than the internally viviparous (cetaceans)
measurable_quantities: presence or absence of testes in male fishes and snakes
claims.candidate_data: Comparative reproductive anatomy annotated in Uberon and the Phenoscape Knowledgebase; Animal Diversity Web species accounts.

claims.label: Birds, oviparous quadrupeds and the hedgehog have internal testicles near the loin
claims.claim: Birds have testicles placed internally close to the loin, as do oviparous quadrupeds such as the lizard, the tortoise and the crocodile, and among viviparous animals the hedgehog.
claims.quote: Birds are furnished with testicles, but these are internally situated, close to the loin. The case is similar with oviparous quadrupeds, such as the lizard, the tortoise and the crocodile; and among the viviparous animals this peculiarity is found in the hedgehog.
claims.scope: birds; oviparous quadrupeds (lizards, turtles, crocodilians); hedgehog
measurable_quantities: position of the testes (internal, near kidneys) in birds, reptiles and hedgehogs
claims.candidate_data: Comparative anatomy in Uberon and the Phenoscape Knowledgebase; literature on testicular descent across mammals; Animal Diversity Web.

claims.label: Bird testicles enlarge greatly in the breeding season
claims.claim: Before the breeding season the testicles of birds are small or invisible, but during the breeding season they become greatly enlarged in all birds.
claims.quote: before the breeding season the organ is small in some birds and quite invisible in others, but during the season the organ in all cases is greatly enlarged.
claims.scope: birds, notably the ring-dove and the partridge
measurable_quantities: testis mass or volume in and out of the breeding season
claims.candidate_data: Published measurements of seasonal gonadal recrudescence in birds; avian reproductive physiology literature.

claims.label: Selachians are internally oviparous and externally viviparous
claims.claim: The dogfish and the other selachians (footless gilled animals that bear live young) produce eggs inside the body, and the eggs turn into young within the womb before birth.
claims.quote: With animals devoid of feet that are internally oviparous and viviparous externally, as is the case with the dogfish and the other so-called Selachians
measurable_quantities: reproductive mode (oviparity, aplacental or placental viviparity) per species
claims.candidate_data: Reproductive mode fields in FishBase; chondrichthyan life-history compilations.

claims.label: The viper is the only viviparous serpent
claims.claim: Serpents as a rule lay eggs; the viper is the only serpent that bears live young, and it does so by first producing eggs internally.
claims.quote: Serpents as a rule are oviparous, the viper being the only viviparous member of the genus. The viper is, previously to external parturition, oviparous internally
measurable_quantities: reproductive mode (oviparous or viviparous) across snake species
claims.candidate_data: The Reptile Database species accounts and published squamate reproductive-mode compilations.

claims.label: Horned animals, hare, mouse and bat have cotyledons in the pregnant womb
claims.claim: Pregnant females of horned animals lacking upper front teeth have cotyledons in the womb, as do the hare, the mouse and the bat; all other viviparous footed animals with teeth in both jaws have a smooth womb with the embryo attached directly to it.
claims.quote: the females of horned nonambidental animals are furnished with cotyledons in the womb when they are pregnant, and such is the case, among ambidentals, with the hare, the mouse, and the bat
claims.scope: horned ruminants (non-ambidentals, lacking upper incisors); hare, mouse, bat; other viviparous quadrupeds
measurable_quantities: placental type (cotyledonary, discoid, diffuse, zonary) per species
claims.candidate_data: Comparative placentation data compiled in the literature (e.g. Mossman's survey) and in Phenoscape anatomy annotations.

claims.label: The great blood-vessels originate in the heart, not the head
claims.claim: The two great blood-vessels (the great vein and the aorta) have their origin in the heart, not, as earlier writers held, in the head or brain.
claims.quote: These blood-vessels have their origins in the heart, for they traverse the other viscera, in whatever direction they happen to run, without in any way losing their distinctive characteristic as blood-vessels
measurable_quantities: anatomical origin of the vena cava and aorta
claims.candidate_data: Vertebrate cardiovascular anatomy in Uberon and standard anatomical atlases.

claims.label: The heart has three chambers, all visible only in the largest animals
claims.claim: The heart has three chambers; in small animals even the largest chamber is scarcely visible, in medium-sized animals the second is scarcely visible, and only in the largest animals are all three distinctly seen.
claims.quote: In the case of the smaller animals even the largest of the chambers is scarcely discernible; the second larger is scarcely discernible in animals of medium size; but in the largest animals all three chambers are distinctly seen.
measurable_quantities: number of heart chambers across vertebrate taxa
relation of chamber visibility to body size
claims.candidate_data: Comparative cardiac anatomy in Uberon and Phenoscape; body mass from AnAge or PanTHERIA.

claims.label: The brain contains no blood and no vein
claims.claim: In all animals the brain itself is bloodless, and no vein, large or small, runs within it; veins end in the membrane around the brain.
claims.quote: The brain itself in all animals is destitute of blood, and no vein, great or small, holds its course therein.
measurable_quantities: presence of blood vessels within brain tissue
claims.candidate_data: Neurovascular anatomy in standard anatomical atlases and Uberon.

claims.label: Fibres in the blood cause it to coagulate
claims.claim: Blood coagulates because of a fibrous matter it contains; if the fibre is left in, the blood coagulates, and if it is removed, the blood cannot coagulate.
claims.quote: If this fibre be left in the blood, the blood will coagulate; if it be removed or extracted, the blood is found to be incapable of coagulation.
measurable_quantities: clotting of whole blood versus defibrinated blood
claims.candidate_data: Standard haematology on defibrination and clotting; comparative coagulation studies.

claims.label: Deer, roe and antelope blood lacks fibre and clots weakly
claims.claim: The blood of the deer, the roe, the antelope and some other animals lacks the coagulating fibre, and so does not coagulate as firmly as the blood of other animals.
claims.quote: we fail to find it in the blood of the deer, the roe, the antelope, and some other animals; and, owing to this deficiency of the fibrous tissue, the blood of these animals does not coagulate to the extent observed in the blood of other animals.
measurable_quantities: plasma fibrinogen concentration
clot firmness in cervid and bovid blood versus other mammals
claims.candidate_data: Veterinary haematology reference intervals for cervids, bovids and leporids (e.g. Species360 ZIMS reference values).

claims.label: The crocodile is the only animal that moves its upper jaw
claims.claim: Animals in general move the lower jaw; the river crocodile is the only animal that moves the upper jaw.
claims.quote: Animals in general move the lower jaw; the river crocodile is the only animal that moves the upper one.
measurable_quantities: mobility of upper jaw relative to skull (cranial kinesis) across taxa
claims.candidate_data: Comparative cranial-kinesis literature on crocodilians, birds and snakes; MorphoSource skull scans.

claims.label: The dolphin has true bone, not fish-spine
claims.claim: The dolphin's skeleton is made of bone, like that of viviparous quadrupeds, not of fish-spine.
claims.quote: The dolphin has bones, and not fish-spine.
measurable_quantities: skeletal tissue type in cetaceans
claims.candidate_data: Cetacean osteology and skeletal scans in MorphoSource; Uberon tissue annotations.

claims.label: Only the stag has solid branching horns, shed annually unless castrated
claims.claim: Of all animals only the stag has horns that are solid throughout and branched, and only the deer sheds its horns, annually, unless it has been castrated.
claims.quote: In the case of the stag alone of all animals the horns are solid throughout, and ramify into branches (or antlers). And, whereas no other animal is known to shed its horns, the deer sheds its horns annually, unless it has been castrated
measurable_quantities: antler versus horn structure
annual antler casting
antler cycle in castrated males
claims.candidate_data: Cervid antler-cycle and castration literature; Animal Diversity Web accounts of horned ungulates.

claims.label: All toed animals have nails except the elephant
claims.claim: All animals that have feet with toes have nails, except the elephant, whose toes are undivided and slightly jointed and which has no nails at all.
claims.quote: all animals have nails that have toes, and toes that have feet, except the elephant; and the elephant has toes undivided and slightly articulated, but has no nails whatsoever
measurable_quantities: presence of nails or hoof-like nails on elephant feet
nails or claws across toed taxa
claims.candidate_data: Elephant foot anatomy literature; Phenoscape integumentary appendage annotations.

claims.label: Viviparous footed animals have hair, oviparous footed have scutes, fishes scales
claims.claim: All viviparous animals with feet have hair; all oviparous animals with feet have horny plates; and fishes, and only fishes, have scales.
claims.quote: All viviparous animals furnished with feet have hair; all oviparous animals furnished with feet have horn-like tessellates; fishes, and fishes only, have scales
measurable_quantities: integument type (hair, scutes, scales) by taxon and reproductive mode
claims.candidate_data: Phenoscape integument annotations; reproductive mode from AmphiBIO and the Reptile Database; Open Tree of Life for coverage.

claims.label: Grey hairs are mostly white from the start, so greying is not withering
claims.claim: Hair greys from the tip back toward the root, but most grey hairs are white from the beginning, which shows that greying is not a withering or decrepitude of the hair.
claims.quote: Hair turns grey from the point backwards to the roots. But, in the majority of cases, grey hairs are white from the beginning; and this is a proof that greyness of hair does not, as some believe to be the case, imply withering or decrepitude
measurable_quantities: pigmentation along the length of greying hair shafts
claims.candidate_data: Dermatological studies of hair-shaft pigmentation and greying.

claims.label: Boys, women and castrated men never go bald
claims.claim: No boy, no woman and no castrated man ever becomes bald, and a man castrated before puberty never grows the later hair (pubic, axillary, beard).
claims.quote: For no boy ever gets bald, no woman, and no castrated man. In fact, if a man be castrated before reaching puberty, the later growths of hair never come at all
measurable_quantities: incidence of baldness in prepubertal boys, women and castrated men
secondary hair growth after prepubertal castration
claims.candidate_data: Clinical literature on androgenetic alopecia and on eunuchs (e.g. Hamilton's studies of castrated men).

claims.label: The crane is the only bird that changes colour with age
claims.claim: No bird changes colour by reason of age except the crane, whose wings are ash-coloured at first and turn black as it grows old.
claims.quote: no creature is liable to change of colour by reason of age, excepting the crane. The wings of this bird are ash-coloured at first, but as it grows old the wings get black.
measurable_quantities: age-related plumage colour change across bird species
claims.candidate_data: Age-specific plumage descriptions in ornithological handbooks and the Birds of the World accounts.

claims.label: Drinking water can make rams beget black lambs
claims.claim: In many places the drinking water is of such a quality that rams that drink it before mating beget black lambs.
claims.quote: water in many places is of such peculiar quality that rams, if they have intercourse with the female after drinking it, beget black lambs
measurable_quantities: lamb coat colour in relation to sire's drinking water source
claims.candidate_data: Sheep coat-colour inheritance literature; controlled breeding records.

claims.label: Blood forms first in the heart before the body is differentiated
claims.claim: In development, blood appears first in the heart, before the body as a whole is differentiated.
claims.quote: Blood is developed first of all in the heart of animals before the body is differentiated as a whole.
measurable_quantities: timing and site of first blood formation relative to body patterning in embryos
claims.candidate_data: Developmental staging data for chick and mouse embryos; embryological literature on haematopoiesis.

claims.label: All internally and externally viviparous animals, including cetaceans, have breasts
claims.claim: All animals that are viviparous both internally and externally, including all hairy animals and the cetaceans (dolphin, porpoise, whale), have breasts and milk; oviparous animals and those only externally viviparous have neither.
claims.quote: All animals have breasts that are internally and externally viviparous, as for instance all animals that have hair, as man and the horse; and the cetaceans, as the dolphin, the porpoise, and the whale-for these animals have breasts and are supplied with milk.
claims.scope: viviparous animals (mammals, including cetaceans); fishes and birds
measurable_quantities: presence of mammary glands and lactation by taxon
claims.candidate_data: Phenoscape and Uberon mammary gland annotations; Animal Diversity Web.

claims.label: Camel's milk is thinnest, then human, then ass; cow's milk is thickest
claims.claim: Of milks, the camel's is the thinnest, human milk next, then the ass's, and cow's milk is the thickest.
claims.quote: Now the camel's milk is the thinnest, and that of the human species next after it, and that of the ass next again, but cow's milk is the thickest.
measurable_quantities: milk solids, fat and casein content by species
claims.candidate_data: Published comparative milk composition tables for mammals (e.g. the Oftedal milk composition data).

claims.label: Fertile sperm sinks in water, infertile sperm dissolves
claims.claim: Sperm capable of impregnating sinks in water, while infertile sperm dissolves away.
claims.quote: Sperm capable of impregnating or of fructification sinks in water; sperm incapable Of producing that result dissolves away.
claims.scope: animals with blood (all of which emit sperm)
measurable_quantities: behaviour of fertile versus infertile semen samples in water
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Molluscs have eight feet with two rows of suckers, save one octopus
claims.claim: All molluscs (cephalopods) have eight feet, each with a double row of suckers, except one species of octopus.
claims.quote: All molluscs are furnished with eight feet, and in all cases these feet are severally furnished with a double row of suckers, with the exception of one single species of poulpe or octopus.
claims.scope: molluscs in Aristotle's sense (cephalopods: octopus, cuttlefish, squid); the heledone (Eledone)
measurable_quantities: arm number
number of sucker rows per arm by cephalopod species
claims.candidate_data: SeaLifeBase cephalopod species accounts; cephalopod taxonomic literature.

claims.label: The octopus copulates with a special arm
claims.claim: The octopus uses its last arm for copulation, and that arm is sharp, whitish and forked at its tip.
claims.quote: the last of his feelers he employs in the act of copulation; and this last one, by the way, is extremely sharp, is exceptional as being of a whitish colour, and at its extremity is bifurcate
measurable_quantities: presence and form of a hectocotylized arm in male octopuses
claims.candidate_data: Cephalopod reproductive anatomy literature; SeaLifeBase species accounts.

claims.label: All cephalopods discharge ink when frightened, the cuttlefish most
claims.claim: All molluscs (cephalopods) discharge a black juice when frightened, and the cuttlefish discharges it most copiously.
claims.quote: All molluscs, when frightened, discharge such a juice, but the discharge is most copious in the cuttle-fish.
measurable_quantities: presence and size of ink sac
ink release in response to threat
claims.candidate_data: Cephalopod anatomy and behaviour literature; SeaLifeBase.

claims.label: Crawfish and crabs have ten feet including the claws
claims.claim: The crawfish has five feet on each side including the claws, and the crab likewise has ten feet in all including the claws.
claims.quote: The crawfishes have five feet on either side, including the claws at the end; and in like manner the crabs have ten feet in all, including the claws.
measurable_quantities: number of walking legs including chelipeds
claims.candidate_data: Decapod morphology in SeaLifeBase and the World Register of Marine Species.

claims.label: Lobsters always have one claw larger than the other, in both sexes
claims.claim: In the lobster both male and female have one claw larger than the other, and no lobster of either sex is ever found with both claws the same size.
claims.quote: There is no apparent difference between the male and female, for they both have one claw, whichever it may be, larger than the other, and neither male nor female is ever found with both claws of the same size.
measurable_quantities: claw asymmetry in male and female lobsters
claims.candidate_data: Studies of cheliped asymmetry (crusher and cutter claws) in Homarus.

claims.label: Crabs mostly have the right claw larger
claims.claim: Crabs for the most part have the right claw bigger and stronger than the left.
claims.quote: for the most part they have the right claw bigger and stronger than the left.
measurable_quantities: proportion of right-handed versus left-handed claw asymmetry in crab populations
claims.candidate_data: Published field surveys of cheliped handedness in brachyuran crabs.

claims.label: Spiral-shelled testaceans all coil to the right
claims.claim: All spiral-shelled testaceans have their shells on the right-hand side and move in the direction opposite to the spire.
claims.quote: all stromboid testaceans have their shells on the right hand side, and move not in the direction of the spire, but the opposite way.
measurable_quantities: proportion of dextral versus sinistral coiling across gastropod species
claims.candidate_data: Gastropod shell-chirality surveys; MolluscaBase and the World Register of Marine Species.

claims.label: Murex and trumpet-shell bore through other shells with a proboscis
claims.claim: The purple murex and the trumpet-shell have a firm proboscis with which they bore right through the shells of the shellfish they prey on.
claims.quote: so is that proboscis proportionately stronger in these testaceans; for they bore right through the shells of other shell-fish on which they prey.
measurable_quantities: drilling predation by muricid gastropods on bivalves
claims.candidate_data: Literature on drilling predation by Muricidae; SeaLifeBase diet records.

claims.label: The hermit crab is intermediate between crustaceans and testaceans
claims.claim: The hermit crab is by nature like the crawfish but lives inside a shell like a testacean, and so is intermediate between crustaceans and testaceans.
claims.quote: In its nature it resembles the crawfish kind, and it is born simple of itself, but by its habit of introducing itself into a shell and living there it resembles the testaceans, and so appears to partake of the characters of both kinds.
claims.candidate_data: Open Tree of Life for the placement of hermit crabs among decapods.

claims.label: The sea-urchin's mouth is below because its food lies below
claims.claim: The sea-urchin has its mouth underneath and its excretory outlet on top because its food lies below, so the mouth is placed where it is best suited to reach the food.
claims.quote: For the food on which the creature lives lies down below; consequently the mouth has a position well adapted for getting at the food, and the excretion is above, near to the back of the shell.
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Sea-urchins always have five egg masses
claims.claim: The sea-urchin always has the same number of so-called eggs, an odd number, namely five, lying beneath the stomach.
claims.quote: Underneath the stomach, in another membrane, are the so-called eggs, identical in number in all cases, and that number is always an odd number, to wit five.
measurable_quantities: number of gonads in sea-urchin species
claims.candidate_data: Echinoid anatomy literature; SeaLifeBase and the World Register of Marine Species.

claims.label: The sea-anemone has no excretion and so resembles a plant
claims.claim: The sea-anemone appears to produce no excretion at all, and in this respect resembles a plant.
claims.quote: The sea-nettle appears to be devoid altogether of excretion, and in this respect it resembles a plant.
measurable_quantities: egestion of undigested material through the mouth in anemones
claims.candidate_data: Cnidarian feeding physiology literature.

claims.label: Insects cut in two continue to live
claims.claim: All insects continue to live when cut in two, except those that are cold by nature or so small that they chill quickly.
claims.quote: All insects when cut in two continue to live, excepting such as are naturally cold by nature, or such as from their minute size chill rapidly
measurable_quantities: survival time and movement of bisected insect and myriapod body parts
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: No two-winged insect has a sting in the rear
claims.claim: No insect with only two wings has a sting at the rear of its body.
claims.quote: no insect with only two wings has a sting in the rear.
measurable_quantities: presence of an abdominal sting in Diptera
claims.candidate_data: Insect morphology databases and Diptera taxonomic literature.

claims.label: The cicada has no mouth and feeds only on dew
claims.claim: The cicada, alone of all creatures, has no mouth but a long tongue-like organ, and with it feeds on dew alone, so that no excrement is ever found in its stomach.
claims.quote: by the aid of this the creature feeds on dew, and on dew only, and in its stomach no excretion is ever found.
measurable_quantities: cicada diet (xylem sap versus dew)
presence of excreta in the gut
claims.candidate_data: Entomological literature on cicada xylem feeding and honeydew/excreta production.

claims.label: There are exactly five senses
claims.claim: There are five senses, sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch, and no other special sense is known.
claims.quote: The total number of the senses (for we have no experience of any special sense not here included), is five: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch.
claims.candidate_data: Comparative sensory biology literature on additional modalities (electroreception, magnetoreception).

claims.label: The mole has complete but stunted eyes hidden under the skin
claims.claim: The mole is blind and has no visible eyes, but under the thick skin of the head it has stunted eyes containing all the parts of ordinary eyes.
claims.quote: the eyes are found inside in a stunted condition, furnished with all the parts found in ordinary eyes
measurable_quantities: eye size and structure under the skin in moles
claims.candidate_data: Anatomical and histological studies of eyes in Talpa and other moles.

claims.label: Fishes hear and smell despite having no visible organs for either
claims.claim: Although fishes have no visible organs of hearing or smell, they undoubtedly hear and smell, as shown by their fleeing from loud noises.
claims.quote: but for all this fishes undoubtedly hear and smell. For they are observed to run away from any loud noise, such as would be made by the rowing of a galley
measurable_quantities: behavioural responses of fish to sound and odour
presence of inner ear and olfactory organs
claims.candidate_data: Fish auditory and olfactory physiology literature.

claims.label: Bloodless animals fall into four genera
claims.claim: With very few exceptions, the animals without blood fall into four kinds: molluscs (cephalopods), crustaceans, testaceans (shelled molluscs and the like) and insects.
claims.quote: All other animals may, with very few exceptions, be comprehended within four genera: to wit, molluscs, crustaceans, testaceans, and insects.
claims.candidate_data: Open Tree of Life for comparing the grouping with modern invertebrate phylogeny.

claims.label: Animals without lungs have no voice
claims.claim: No animal can produce voice except by the action of the pharynx, so animals without lungs have no voice.
claims.quote: no animal can give utterance to voice except by the action of the pharynx, and consequently such animals as are devoid of lung have no voice
measurable_quantities: mechanism of sound production across taxa
claims.candidate_data: Comparative bioacoustics literature on sound production in fishes, insects and tetrapods.

claims.label: No insect breathes
claims.claim: Insects have no voice and make sound by internal air rather than by expelling air, because no insect breathes.
claims.quote: they can emit sound by internal air or wind, though not by the emission of air or wind; for no insects are capable of respiration.
measurable_quantities: gas exchange in insects
mechanisms of insect sound production
claims.candidate_data: Insect respiratory physiology literature on the tracheal system.

claims.label: Language is peculiar to man
claims.claim: Viviparous quadrupeds utter various vocal sounds but cannot converse; language is peculiar to man.
claims.quote: Viviparous quadrupeds utter vocal sounds of different kinds, but they have no power of converse. In fact, this power, or language, is peculiar to man.
measurable_quantities: combinatorial structure of vocal communication across mammals
claims.candidate_data: Comparative animal communication literature.

claims.label: Bird song is learned and varies by locality
claims.claim: Some young birds removed from the nest sing a different note from their parents after hearing other birds, so bird song is not wholly innate but can be modified and improved, and it varies by locality.
claims.quote: Of little birds, some sing a different note from the parent birds, if they have been removed from the nest and have heard other birds singing
measurable_quantities: song of cross-fostered or tutored birds versus parental song
geographic song dialects
claims.candidate_data: Song-learning and dialect studies; recordings in the Macaulay Library and xeno-canto.

claims.label: Horses, dogs, oxen and all viviparous quadrupeds dream
claims.claim: Not only men but horses, dogs, oxen, sheep, goats and all viviparous quadrupeds appear to dream, dogs showing it by barking in their sleep.
claims.quote: it would appear that not only do men dream, but horses also, and dogs, and oxen; aye, and sheep, and goats, and all viviparous quadrupeds; and dogs show their dreaming by barking in their sleep.
measurable_quantities: presence of REM sleep and sleep vocalizations across mammals
claims.candidate_data: Comparative mammalian sleep databases (e.g. the Savage and West sleep compilation) and REM sleep literature.

claims.label: Fishes, cephalopods and crustaceans sleep, but briefly
claims.claim: Water animals such as fishes, molluscs (cephalopods) and crustaceans undoubtedly sleep, though their sleep is very short.
claims.quote: These animals sleep without doubt, although their sleep is of very short duration.
claims.scope: fishes, cephalopods, crustaceans (crawfish and the like)
measurable_quantities: behavioural sleep criteria and sleep duration in fishes, cephalopods and crustaceans
claims.candidate_data: Behavioural sleep studies in zebrafish, octopus and crayfish.

claims.label: Cetaceans sleep with the blow-hole above the water
claims.claim: The dolphin, the whale and all animals with a blow-hole sleep with the blow-hole above the surface, breathing through it while gently moving their fins.
claims.quote: The dolphin and the whale, and all such as are furnished with a blow-hole, sleep with the blow-hole over the surface of the water
measurable_quantities: posture and breathing during sleep in cetaceans
claims.candidate_data: Cetacean sleep studies (logging behaviour, unihemispheric sleep).

claims.label: Sessile animals and testaceans have no separate sexes
claims.claim: Animals that live fixed in one place have no distinction of sex, nor does any testacean.
claims.quote: In animals that live confined to one spot there is no duality of sex; nor is there such, in fact, in any testaceans.
claims.scope: sessile animals; testaceans (shelled molluscs, sea-urchins and the like)
measurable_quantities: sexual system (gonochoric or hermaphroditic) in sessile and shelled invertebrates
claims.candidate_data: Sexual-system compilations for molluscs and echinoderms; SeaLifeBase reproduction fields.

claims.label: The eel is neither male nor female and engenders nothing
claims.claim: The eel is neither male nor female and produces no offspring; no eel has ever been seen with an egg.
claims.quote: For instance, the eel is neither male nor female, and can engender nothing.
measurable_quantities: gonadal sex in eels
presence of eggs in eels
claims.candidate_data: Anguilla reproductive biology literature; FishBase species accounts.

claims.label: The psetta, erythrinus and channe are always found with eggs
claims.claim: Among fishes, the psetta, the erythrinus and the channe are always found bearing eggs, having what bears and engenders but nothing that impregnates.
claims.quote: so is it, among fishes, with the psetta, the erythrinus, and the channe; for these fish are in all cases found furnished with eggs.
claims.scope: psetta, erythrinus, channe (channe is plausibly the comber, Serranus cabrilla)
measurable_quantities: presence of ovarian and testicular tissue in individuals of these species
claims.candidate_data: FishBase reproduction fields; literature on hermaphroditism in Serranus.

claims.label: Males larger in viviparous footed animals, females larger in egg-layers
claims.claim: As a general rule, in viviparous footed animals with blood the male is larger and longer-lived than the female (the mule excepted), whereas in oviparous and larva-producing animals such as fishes and insects the female is larger than the male.
claims.quote: in red-blooded animals furnished with feet and not oviparous, the male is larger and longer-lived than the female (except with the mule, where the female is longer-lived and bigger than the male); whereas in oviparous and vermiparous creatures, as in fishes and in insects, the female is larger than the male
claims.scope: viviparous quadrupeds (mammals) versus fishes, insects, snakes, spiders, geckos, frogs
measurable_quantities: sexual size dimorphism by taxon
sex difference in lifespan
claims.candidate_data: Sex-specific body size and lifespan in AnAge, the Amniote Life-History Database, FishBase and AmphiBIO.

claims.label: Some animals arise by spontaneous generation from putrefying matter
claims.claim: Some animals are born from parents of their own kind, while others arise spontaneously and not from kindred stock, some of them out of putrefying earth or vegetable matter (as many insects do) and others inside animals out of the secretions of their organs.
claims.quote: some spring from parent animals according to their kind, whilst others grow spontaneously and not from kindred stock; and of these instances of spontaneous generation some come from putrefying earth or vegetable matter, as is the case with a number of insects
claims.scope: animals generally, especially insects and internal parasites
measurable_quantities: whether any animal arises from putrefying matter without parents (sterile-medium exclusion experiments)
claims.candidate_data: Classic exclusion experiments (Redi, Spallanzani, Pasteur) and life-cycle records for insects and parasites in the Animal Diversity Web.

claims.label: Female cartilaginous fishes are larger than males
claims.claim: In the cartilaginous fishes (selachians) the female is larger than the male, and the same holds for most other fishes.
claims.quote: In the cartilaginous species the female is larger than the male; and the same is the case with other fishes for the most part.
claims.scope: selachians (sharks, rays, skates) and fishes generally
measurable_quantities: female vs male maximum or mean body length by species
claims.candidate_data: Sex-specific maximum lengths and length at maturity in FishBase.

claims.label: Male sharks and dogfish have two appendages near the vent
claims.claim: In cartilaginous fishes the male, unlike the female, has two appendages hanging down near the vent, and this sex difference is found in all species of sharks and dogfish.
claims.quote: in cartilaginous fishes the male, in some species, differs from the female in the fact that he is furnished with two appendages hanging down from about the exit of the residuum, and that the female is not so furnished
measurable_quantities: presence of paired pelvic claspers in males and absence in females across shark species
claims.candidate_data: Comparative anatomy of chondrichthyan claspers in Phenoscape and Uberon; species accounts in FishBase.

claims.label: Fishes and footless animals lack testicles but have paired sperm ducts
claims.claim: Neither fishes nor any footless animals have testicles; instead male serpents and male fishes have a pair of ducts that fill with milt in the breeding season and discharge a milky fluid.
claims.quote: Now neither fishes nor any animals devoid of feet are furnished with testicles, but male serpents and male fishes have a pair of ducts which fill with milt or sperm at the rutting season
measurable_quantities: presence of testes in male fishes and snakes
claims.candidate_data: Gonad anatomy in Uberon and Phenoscape; fish reproductive anatomy summaries in FishBase.

claims.label: Birds and footed egg-layers have internal testicles
claims.claim: Birds have their testicles inside the body, and so do all oviparous animals that have feet.
claims.quote: birds, by the way, have their testicles in their interior, and so have all ovipara that are furnished with feet
measurable_quantities: position of testes (abdominal vs scrotal) across birds, reptiles and amphibians
claims.candidate_data: Testis position in Uberon and Phenoscape; comparative anatomy literature.

claims.label: Non-viviparous animals lack a bladder, except the tortoise
claims.claim: Animals that are not viviparous have no bladder, with the single exception of the tortoise.
claims.quote: these animals are unprovided with a bladder except in the case of the tortoise
measurable_quantities: presence of a urinary bladder across birds, lizards, snakes, turtles, amphibians and fishes
claims.candidate_data: Urinary bladder presence across taxa in Uberon and Phenoscape.

claims.label: A female partridge downwind of the male becomes impregnated
claims.claim: A female partridge becomes impregnated if she gets to leeward of the male, and often merely by hearing his voice or by his breathing on her as he flies overhead.
claims.quote: With partridges, by the way, if the female gets to leeward of the male, she becomes thereby impregnated.
measurable_quantities: fertility of eggs from female partridges isolated from physical contact with males
claims.candidate_data: Poultry and gamebird reproductive physiology literature on fertilization requiring copulation.

claims.label: Cephalopods copulate mouth to mouth by interlacing tentacles
claims.claim: The octopus, the cuttlefish and the squid all mate in the same way, uniting at the mouth by interlacing their tentacles.
claims.quote: Molluscs, such as the octopus, the sepia, and the calamary, have sexual intercourse all in the same way; that is to say, they unite at the mouth, by an interlacing of their tentacles.
measurable_quantities: mating positions recorded for octopus, cuttlefish and squid species
claims.candidate_data: Behavioural observations of cephalopod mating in the literature and species accounts in SeaLifeBase.

claims.label: In insects the female inserts her organ into the male
claims.claim: In copulating insects the female pushes her sexual organ up into the body of the male, the reverse of what happens in other animals.
claims.quote: The female pushes from underneath her sexual organ into the body of the male above, this being the reverse of the operation observed in other creatures
claims.scope: insects, e.g. flies and cantharid beetles
measurable_quantities: direction of genital intromission in insect copulation
claims.candidate_data: Insect genital morphology and copulation studies in the entomological literature.

claims.label: Most animals mate in spring, when winter turns to summer
claims.claim: Animals in general are naturally disposed to mate at about the same time of year, in spring as winter changes into summer, when almost all flying, walking and swimming creatures pair.
claims.quote: Animals in general seem naturally disposed to this intercourse at about the same period of the year, and that is when winter is changing into summer.
measurable_quantities: breeding or mating month by species across taxa
claims.candidate_data: Breeding-season fields in the Amniote Life-History Database, AnAge and FishBase spawning records.

claims.label: The halcyon breeds at the winter solstice
claims.claim: The halcyon (kingfisher) breeds at the time of the winter solstice, unlike nearly all other birds, which breed in spring and early summer.
claims.quote: The halcyon breeds at the season of the winter solstice.
claims.scope: the halcyon (usually identified as the common kingfisher)
measurable_quantities: breeding month of the common kingfisher in the Mediterranean
claims.candidate_data: Breeding phenology of Alcedo atthis in nest-record schemes and the Animal Diversity Web.

claims.label: Most wild animals give birth only once a year
claims.claim: Most wild animals bring forth young once and only once a year, except animals such as the hare whose females can conceive again while already pregnant.
claims.quote: The greater part of wild animals bring forth once and once only in the year, except in the case of animals like the hare, where the female can become superfoetally impregnated.
measurable_quantities: litters or clutches per year by species
occurrence of superfetation in hares
claims.candidate_data: Litters per year in PanTHERIA and the Amniote Life-History Database; superfetation studies in the European brown hare.

claims.label: The pelamys and the tunny breed only in the Black Sea
claims.claim: The pelamys (young tunny or bonito) and the tunny breed in the Black Sea and nowhere else.
claims.quote: The pelamys and the tunny breed in the Euxine, and nowhere else.
claims.scope: tunny (Atlantic bluefin tuna) and pelamys (bonito or young tunny)
measurable_quantities: locations of spawning grounds of bluefin tuna and Atlantic bonito
claims.candidate_data: Spawning-ground records in FishBase and ICCAT bluefin tuna assessments; larval occurrences in GBIF and OBIS.

claims.label: The brooding female octopus stops feeding and loses condition
claims.claim: The female octopus, after laying her eggs, broods over them and loses condition because she does not go out for food during the hatching period.
claims.quote: The female, after laying her eggs, broods over them, and in consequence gets out of condition, by reason of not going in quest of food during the hatching period.
measurable_quantities: feeding rate and body mass of brooding female octopuses
claims.candidate_data: Studies of maternal brooding and post-spawning senescence in Octopus vulgaris; SeaLifeBase species accounts.

claims.label: Sea urchins have most eggs in warm weather and at full moon
claims.claim: The edible sea urchin is never without its so-called eggs, but has them in greatest abundance in spring and autumn, in warm weather, and when the moon is full.
claims.quote: it is furnished with them in especial abundance in warm weather or when a full moon is in the sky
claims.scope: edible sea urchin (probably Paracentrotus lividus); excluding urchins of the Pyrrhaean Straits
measurable_quantities: gonad index of sea urchins by season and lunar phase
claims.candidate_data: Published gonad-index time series for Mediterranean sea urchins and studies of lunar spawning periodicity.

claims.label: Wild birds breed once a year; the swallow and blackbird twice
claims.claim: Wild birds as a rule pair and breed only once a year, but the swallow and the blackbird breed twice.
claims.quote: Of birds the wild species, as has been stated, as a general rule pair and breed only once a year. The swallow, however, and the blackbird breed twice.
measurable_quantities: broods per year by bird species
claims.candidate_data: Broods-per-year fields in the Amniote Life-History Database and national nest-record schemes.

claims.label: Ring-dove is the largest pigeon, the turtle-dove the smallest
claims.claim: Among the pigeons the ring-dove is the largest, the stock-dove next and a little larger than the common pigeon, and the turtle-dove the smallest.
claims.quote: The largest of all the pigeon species is the phatta or ring-dove; and the next in size is the oenas or stock-dove; and the stock-dove is a little larger than the common pigeon. The smallest of all the species is the turtle-dove.
claims.scope: Greek columbids: wood pigeon, stock dove, rock/domestic pigeon, turtle dove
measurable_quantities: body mass and wing length of Columba palumbus, C. oenas, C. livia and Streptopelia turtur
claims.candidate_data: Body mass and morphometrics in AVONET and the Amniote Life-History Database.

claims.label: The first semen produced is infertile or yields poor offspring
claims.claim: In all animals the earliest semen produced is infertile, or if fertile gives smaller and poorer offspring, as seen especially in man, viviparous quadrupeds and birds (whose first eggs are smaller).
claims.quote: in all animals, the earliest secretion of sperm is unfruitful, or if it be fruitful the issue is comparatively poor and small
claims.scope: copulating animals, especially man, viviparous quadrupeds and birds
measurable_quantities: fertility and offspring size by parental age at first reproduction
egg size of first clutches vs later clutches
claims.candidate_data: Livestock and poultry breeding records on young-sire fertility and pullet egg size; human andrology studies of adolescent semen.

claims.label: Men produce semen at about fourteen and are fertile at about twenty-one
claims.claim: A man begins to produce seminal fluid at about fourteen years of age and becomes capable of generation at about twenty-one.
claims.quote: Man begins to possess seminal fluid about the age of fourteen, and becomes generatively capable at about the age of twenty-one years.
measurable_quantities: age at spermarche
age at which male fertility is established
claims.candidate_data: Human pubertal development and spermarche studies in the clinical literature.

claims.label: Females and young animals have higher-pitched voices than males and adults
claims.claim: As a general rule the female has a higher-pitched voice than the male, and the young animal than the older one.
claims.quote: As a general rule the female is sharper-toned in voice than the male, and the young animal than the elder
claims.scope: vocal animals, e.g. deer, dogs, horses, humans
measurable_quantities: fundamental frequency of calls by sex and age
claims.candidate_data: Bioacoustic recordings in the Macaulay Library and xeno-canto, and published studies of vocal pitch by sex and age.

claims.label: In cattle the cow's voice is deeper than the bull's
claims.claim: In cattle, contrary to the general rule, the cow has a deeper voice than the bull, and calves a deeper voice than grown cattle.
claims.quote: the cow has a deeper note than the bull, and the calves a deeper note than the cattle
measurable_quantities: fundamental frequency of vocalizations of cows, bulls and calves
claims.candidate_data: Bioacoustic studies of cattle vocalizations by sex and age.

claims.label: Castrated males take on female characters, including voice
claims.claim: Male animals that are castrated take on the characters of the female, which explains the change of voice in gelded animals.
claims.quote: And we can thus understand the change of voice in animals that undergo gelding; for male animals that undergo this process assume the characters of the female.
measurable_quantities: voice pitch and secondary sexual characters in castrated vs intact males
claims.candidate_data: Veterinary and endocrinological studies of castration effects in livestock.

claims.label: The bitch's gestation lasts sixty to sixty-three days
claims.claim: Gestation in the dog lasts sixty to sixty-three days and never less than sixty, or if less the litter does not survive.
claims.quote: The period of gestation with the bitch is sixty days, or sixty-one, or sixty-two, or sixty-three at the utmost
measurable_quantities: gestation length in dogs (days)
claims.candidate_data: Gestation length for Canis familiaris in AnAge, PanTHERIA and veterinary breeding records.

claims.label: Stallions live about thirty-five years, mares a little over forty
claims.claim: The stallion as a rule lives about thirty-five years and the mare a little over forty, so that horses remain sexually capable almost all their lives.
claims.quote: the stallion, as a rule, lives for about thirty-five years, and the mare for a little over forty
measurable_quantities: typical and maximum lifespan of horses by sex
claims.candidate_data: Maximum and typical longevity of Equus caballus in AnAge and equine demographic studies.

claims.label: Men are generative to about sixty-five, women conceive to about forty-five
claims.claim: As a rule a man can beget children up to about sixty-five and a woman can conceive up to about forty-five; at most the limits are seventy and fifty, and these are rare.
claims.quote: As a rule, the male is generative up to the age of sixty-five, and to the age of forty-five the female is capable of conception.
measurable_quantities: age at last birth for women
paternal age distribution at oldest paternity
claims.candidate_data: Natural-fertility demographic data (e.g. Hutterite records) and menopause-age studies.

claims.label: Camel gestation lasts twelve months with a single young
claims.claim: The camel carries its young for twelve months and never bears more than one at a time.
claims.quote: Its period of gestation is twelve months; and it is never delivered of more than one foal at a time.
measurable_quantities: gestation length and litter size in Camelus dromedarius
claims.candidate_data: Gestation length and litter size in AnAge and PanTHERIA.

claims.label: Elephant gestation lasts two years with a single calf
claims.claim: The female elephant carries her young for two years and bears only one at a time.
claims.quote: The period of gestation with the female is two years; and only one young animal is produced at a time, in other words it is uniparous.
measurable_quantities: gestation length and litter size in elephants
claims.candidate_data: Gestation length and litter size for Elephas maximus and Loxodonta africana in AnAge and PanTHERIA.

claims.label: The murex lives about six years, with yearly growth marked on its shell
claims.claim: The purple murex lives about six years, and each year's growth is marked by a distinct interval in the spiral of its shell.
claims.quote: The murex lives for about six years; and the yearly increase is indicated by a distinct interval in the spiral convolution of the shell.
measurable_quantities: lifespan of murex snails
periodicity of shell growth marks (annual or not)
claims.candidate_data: Sclerochronology and age-growth studies of Mediterranean murex species; SeaLifeBase life-history fields.

claims.label: The pinna dies if deprived of its pinna-guard crab or shrimp
claims.claim: The pinna (fan mussel) houses a small shrimp or crab, the pinna-guard, and if it loses this companion it soon dies.
claims.quote: these creatures have inside them a parasite nicknamed the pinna-guard, in some cases a small carid and in other cases a little crab; if the pinna be deprived of this pinna-guard it soon dies
claims.scope: Pinna nobilis and its commensal shrimps and pea crabs
measurable_quantities: survival of fan mussels with and without commensal decapods
claims.candidate_data: Studies of Pinna nobilis symbionts (Pontonia, Nepinnotheres); SeaLifeBase.

claims.label: All testaceans are spontaneously generated in mud, according to the material
claims.claim: As a general rule all testaceans (shelled molluscs and the like) arise by spontaneous generation in mud, and differ according to the material: oysters in slime, cockles on sandy bottoms, ascidians, barnacles and limpets in rock hollows.
claims.quote: As a general rule, then, all testaceans grow by spontaneous generation in mud, differing from one another according to the differences of the material
claims.scope: testaceans: oysters, cockles, mussels, scallops, limpets, ascidians, barnacles
measurable_quantities: presence of spawning, larvae and parental origin in bivalves, gastropods, barnacles and ascidians
claims.candidate_data: Life-cycle and larval-stage records for marine invertebrates in SeaLifeBase and the Animal Diversity Web.

claims.label: Eggs of crustaceans, molluscs and oviparous fishes grow after laying
