claims.label: The trochilus cleans the crocodile's teeth
claims.claim: When the crocodile gapes, a small bird, the trochilus, enters its mouth and cleans its teeth, feeding itself thereby, and the crocodile does not harm it.
claims.quote: When the crocodile yawns, the trochilus flies into his mouth and cleans his teeth. The trochilus gets his food thereby, and the crocodile gets ease and comfort; it makes no attempt to injure its little friend
claims.scope: Nile crocodile and the trochilus (a small Egyptian bird)
measurable_quantities: documented observations of birds feeding inside crocodile mouths
claims.candidate_data: Field observations of Nile crocodile basking behaviour and associated birds; the Animal Diversity Web species accounts.

claims.label: Pigeons pair for life
claims.claim: Pigeons pair with the same mate until one of the pair dies, though occasionally a female mates with a bird other than her mate.
claims.quote: In pairing the same male and the same female keep together; and the union is only broken by the death of one of the two parties.
claims.scope: pigeons and doves (tame pigeon, ring-dove, turtle-dove)
measurable_quantities: pair-bond duration
rates of divorce and extra-pair paternity in Columbidae
claims.candidate_data: Studies of pair-bond fidelity and extra-pair paternity in columbids; Birds of the World species accounts.

claims.label: Heavy-bodied birds like quails and partridges build no nests
claims.claim: Heavy-bodied birds such as quails and partridges build no nests but lay in a scraped hollow on level ground, since nest building would be of no use to birds that cannot fly well.
claims.quote: Birds of a heavy build, such as quails, partridges, and the like, build no nests; indeed, where they are incapable of flight, it would be of no use if they could do so.
claims.scope: heavy-bodied ground birds (quails, partridges and similar galliforms)
measurable_quantities: nest type (scrape versus built nest) versus body mass and flight ability
claims.candidate_data: Nest-type compilations in Birds of the World with body mass and wing shape from AVONET.

claims.label: Partridge hens feign lameness to lure intruders from the brood
claims.claim: When a man comes upon a partridge brood, the hen rolls in front of him pretending to be lame, drawing him away until the young have escaped, then returns and calls them back.
claims.quote: When a man comes by chance upon a young brood, and tries to catch them, the hen-bird rolls in front of the hunter, pretending to be lame: the man every moment thinks he is on the point of catching her, and so she draws him on and on, until every one of her brood has had time to escape
measurable_quantities: occurrence of distraction (injury-feigning) displays in galliforms
claims.candidate_data: Comparative reviews of distraction displays in birds and Birds of the World species accounts.

claims.label: Web-footed birds all live near water
claims.claim: All web-footed birds live near the sea, rivers or pools, because they resort to places suited to their structure.
claims.quote: Web-footed birds without exception live near the sea or rivers or pools, as they naturally resort to places adapted to their structure.
claims.scope: web-footed birds (ducks, geese, swans, gulls and similar)
measurable_quantities: habitat association of species with webbed feet
claims.candidate_data: Foot morphology and habitat data in AVONET and Birds of the World.

claims.label: Swans sing chiefly as they approach death
claims.claim: Swans are musical and sing chiefly at the approach of death, flying out to sea at that time.
claims.quote: They are musical, and sing chiefly at the approach of death; at this time they fly out to sea, and men, when sailing past the coast of Libya, have fallen in with many of them out at sea singing in mournful strains
measurable_quantities: vocalization rate of swans near death
occurrence of swans far out at sea
claims.candidate_data: Swan vocalization recordings in xeno-canto and the Macaulay Library; Birds of the World species accounts.

claims.label: The cuckoo lays a single egg in another bird's nest and does not hatch it
claims.claim: The cuckoo builds no nest, lays only one egg in the nest of another bird, and leaves the foster mother to hatch and rear it.
claims.quote: it lays only one egg and does not hatch it itself, but the mother-bird in whose nest it has deposited it hatches and rears it
claims.scope: common cuckoo (Cuculus canorus) and its hosts (ring-dove, lark, hypolais, green linnet)
measurable_quantities: number of cuckoo eggs per host nest
host species parasitized
claims.candidate_data: Brood-parasitism host records and nest-record schemes such as the BTO Nest Record Scheme.

claims.label: Cuckoos lay in others' nests because of their own cowardice
claims.claim: The cuckoo places its young in another bird's nest because it is the most cowardly of birds and could not defend its young in an emergency.
claims.quote: The cuckoo shows great sagacity in the disposal of its progeny; the fact is, the mother cuckoo is quite conscious of her own cowardice and of the fact that she could never help her young one in an emergency
measurable_quantities: nest-defence behaviour of cuckoos versus related non-parasitic species
claims.candidate_data: None known that directly bears on motive; comparative studies of the evolution of brood parasitism.

claims.label: A pair of eagles needs a large territory and drives other birds away
claims.claim: A pair of eagles needs an extensive area to maintain itself, so it expels its fledged young from the neighbourhood and does not allow other birds to settle nearby.
claims.quote: The fact is that a pair of eagles demands an extensive space for its maintenance, and consequently cannot allow other birds to quarter themselves in close neighbourhood.
measurable_quantities: eagle home-range and territory size
nearest-neighbour distances between eagle nests
claims.candidate_data: Raptor telemetry studies of home range and published nest-spacing data for eagles.

claims.label: The sea-eagle makes its young stare at the sun and kills those that cannot
claims.claim: Before its young are fledged the sea-eagle makes them stare at the sun, beats any that refuse, and kills one whose eyes water.
claims.quote: the sea-eagle is very keen-sighted, and before its young are fledged tries to make them stare at the sun, and beats the one that refuses to do so, and twists him back in the sun's direction; and if one of them gets watery eyes in the process, it kills him, and rears the other.
measurable_quantities: parental behaviour toward nestlings in relation to sun exposure
causes of nestling death
claims.candidate_data: Nest-camera studies of white-tailed eagle and osprey parental behaviour.

claims.label: The fishing-frog lures prey with filaments in front of its eyes
claims.claim: The fishing-frog (angler) has long thin filaments with rounded tips in front of its eyes which it raises as bait while hidden in sand and mud, drawing small fish that touch them into its mouth.
claims.quote: The fishing-frog has a set of filaments that project in front of its eyes; they are long and thin like hairs, and are round at the tips; they lie on either side, and are used as baits.
measurable_quantities: presence and use of the illicium as a lure
burial behaviour
claims.candidate_data: FishBase species accounts for Lophius and studies of anglerfish luring behaviour.

claims.label: The torpedo stuns its prey with a shock from its body
claims.claim: The torpedo (electric ray) catches its prey by numbing it with a shock residing in its body, and can numb humans too.
claims.quote: The torpedo narcotizes the creatures that it wants to catch, overpowering them by the power of shock that is resident in its body, and feeds upon them
measurable_quantities: use of electric discharge in prey capture
discharge voltage
claims.candidate_data: FishBase species accounts for Torpedo and electrophysiological studies of electric-organ discharge.

claims.label: The male sheat-fish guards the spawn for forty to fifty days
claims.claim: In the sheat-fish the female leaves after spawning while the male guards the spawn and fry, driving off small fish, for forty or fifty days until the young can escape on their own.
claims.quote: contenting himself with keeping off all other little fishes that might steal the spawn or fry, and this he does for forty or fifty days, until the young are sufficiently grown to make away from the other fishes for themselves.
measurable_quantities: sex of guarding parent
duration of paternal guarding in days
claims.candidate_data: FishBase species account for Silurus aristotelis and published studies of its paternal care.

claims.label: All fish are carnivorous except a few, and carnivorous fish wander most
claims.claim: All fish are carnivorous except a few such as the grey mullet, the saupe, the red mullet and the chalcis, and the carnivorous fish wander most.
claims.quote: Carnivorous fish wander most; and all fish are carnivorous with the exception of a few, such as the mullet, the saupe, the red mullet, and the chalcis.
measurable_quantities: proportion of fish species with animal-dominated diets
movement range versus trophic level
claims.candidate_data: Diet and trophic-level data in FishBase, with movement and migration data from tagging studies.

claims.label: Only the sepia uses its ink for concealment; octopus and squid ink from fear
claims.claim: Among cephalopods the sepia (cuttlefish) alone discharges its ink for concealment as well as from fear, while the octopus and calamary (squid) discharge it only from fear.
claims.quote: Of molluscs the sepia is the most cunning, and is the only species that employs its dark liquid for the sake of concealment as well as from fear: the octopus and calamary make the discharge solely from fear.
measurable_quantities: contexts of ink release (anti-predator decoy, concealment, hunting) by taxon
claims.candidate_data: Behavioural studies of inking in cephalopods and SeaLifeBase species accounts.

claims.label: The octopus changes colour to match nearby stones
claims.claim: The octopus hunts by changing its colour to match the adjacent stones, and does so also when alarmed.
claims.quote: It seeks its prey by so changing its colour as to render it like the colour of the stones adjacent to it; it does so also when alarmed.
measurable_quantities: background-matching colour change during hunting and alarm
claims.candidate_data: Studies of cephalopod camouflage and background matching; SeaLifeBase.

claims.label: The octopus as a rule does not live beyond one year
claims.claim: The octopus as a rule does not live a full year, and after spawning the female in particular becomes weak, stupid and wastes away.
claims.quote: The octopus as a rule does not live the year out.
measurable_quantities: octopus lifespan
post-spawning senescence and mortality
claims.candidate_data: Age and growth studies of Octopus vulgaris and SeaLifeBase life-history data.

claims.label: The argonaut uses its web as a sail and arms as oars
claims.claim: The nautilus (argonaut) rises to the surface and, when a breeze blows, uses a thin web between its arms as a sail and lets down some arms as rudder-oars.
claims.quote: It uses this structure, when a breeze is blowing, for a sail, and lets down some of its feelers alongside as rudder-oars.
measurable_quantities: observed surface sailing behaviour in Argonauta
claims.candidate_data: Behavioural observations of Argonauta in the wild and SeaLifeBase species accounts.

claims.label: Spiders spin from the surface of the body, not from an excretion
claims.claim: Spiders can spin from birth, and their thread comes off the body like bark rather than from inside as a superfluity or excretion, contrary to Democritus.
claims.quote: Spiders can spin webs from the time of their birth, not from their interior as a superfluity or excretion, as Democritus avers, but off their body as a kind of tree-bark
measurable_quantities: anatomical origin of silk (internal glands versus body surface)
age at onset of silk production
claims.candidate_data: Spider silk-gland anatomy and developmental studies in the arachnology literature.

claims.label: On each trip a bee visits flowers of only one kind
claims.claim: On each foraging trip a bee goes from flower to flower of one kind only and does not visit another kind until it has returned to the hive.
claims.quote: On each expedition the bee does not fly from a flower of one kind to a flower of another, but flies from one violet, say, to another violet, and never meddles with another flower until it has got back to the hive
measurable_quantities: flower constancy: proportion of single-species pollen loads per foraging trip
claims.candidate_data: Pollen-load analyses and flower-constancy studies in honey bees.

claims.label: Bees kill most of their kings to prevent the hive splitting
claims.claim: Worker bees kill most of their kings, especially inferior ones, to prevent a multiplicity of kings from splitting the hive, and destroy royal cells when no swarm is intended.
claims.quote: These bees also kill without mercy most of their kings, and especially kings of the inferior sort; and this they do for fear a multiplicity of kings should lead to a dismemberment of the hive.
measurable_quantities: fate of supernumerary queens and queen cells
relation to swarming
claims.candidate_data: Apicultural studies of queen-cell destruction, queen duels and swarming.

claims.label: A bee that stings dies because it loses its gut with the sting
claims.claim: A bee that stings dies because it cannot withdraw its sting without tearing out its intestines; once it loses its sting it must die.
claims.quote: Bees that sting die from their inability to extract the sting without at the same time extracting their intestines.
measurable_quantities: sting autotomy and post-sting survival of workers
claims.candidate_data: Studies of sting autotomy and post-sting mortality in Apis mellifera.

claims.label: Older bees work indoors, younger bees forage outside
claims.claim: Older bees do the work inside the hive and are rough and hairy from staying indoors, while young bees do the carrying outside and are comparatively smooth.
claims.quote: The elder bees do the indoor work, and are rough and hairy from staying indoors; the young bees do the outer carrying, and are comparatively smooth.
measurable_quantities: age of workers performing in-hive tasks versus foraging
hairiness by worker age
claims.candidate_data: Age-polyethism studies with marked honey bee workers.

claims.label: Bees carry a stone as ballast in high wind
claims.claim: In a high wind bees carry a stone as ballast to steady their flight.
claims.quote: In a high wind they carry a stone by way of ballast to steady them.
measurable_quantities: observations of bees carrying stones or grit in windy conditions
claims.candidate_data: Studies of honey bee flight and foraging under wind.

claims.label: Worker wasps all die in winter; only the mother-wasps overwinter
claims.claim: Worker wasps do not survive into a second year but all die as winter comes on, while the larger mother-wasps survive the winter in holes underground.
claims.quote: The workers do not live over into a second year, but all die when winter comes on; and this can be proved, for at the commencement of winter the workers become drowsy, and about the time of the winter solstice they are never seen at all.
measurable_quantities: worker survival through winter
overwintering caste and site
claims.candidate_data: Life-history studies of temperate social wasps documenting colony cycle and queen hibernation.

claims.label: Lions attack humans when old and their teeth are diseased
claims.claim: Lions invade cattle-folds and attack humans when old age and diseased teeth prevent them from catching their usual prey.
claims.quote: They invade the cattle-folds and attack human beings when they are grown old and so by reason of old age and the diseased condition of their teeth are unable to pursue their wonted prey.
measurable_quantities: age and dental condition of man-eating and livestock-raiding lions
claims.candidate_data: Studies of man-eating lions examining skulls and teeth, and records of livestock depredation by lion age.

claims.label: The elephant breathes through its trunk to cross water
claims.claim: The elephant can make its way through water as long as the tip of its trunk is above the surface, because it breathes through its trunk.
claims.quote: he can make his way through water, as long as the tip of his trunk can be above the surface, for he blows with his trunk and breathes through it.
measurable_quantities: observations of elephants crossing deep water using the trunk as a snorkel
claims.candidate_data: Field observations of elephant swimming and Animal Diversity Web species accounts.

claims.label: Hens that beat a cock become cock-like, even growing spurs
claims.claim: Hens that have beaten the cock in a fight crow like a cock, try to tread him, raise a crest and tail-feathers, and sometimes grow small spurs.
claims.quote: Hens, for instance, when they have beaten the cock in a fight, will crow like the cock and endeavour to tread him; the crest rises up on their head and the tail-feathers on the rump, so that it becomes difficult to recognize that they are hens; in some cases there is a growth of small spurs.
measurable_quantities: incidence of male-like plumage, crowing and spurs in hens
association with dominance
claims.candidate_data: Poultry science literature on spontaneous sex reversal and masculinization in hens.

claims.label: Castrated cocks lose their crest colour, crowing and sexual drive
claims.claim: A full-grown cock castrated by cauterizing the rump loses the colour of its crest, stops crowing and loses sexual desire; if castrated young, it never develops these male traits.
claims.quote: If you burn this twice or thrice with hot irons, then, if the bird be full-grown, his crest grows sallow, he ceases to crow, and foregoes sexual passion; but if you cauterize the bird when young, none of these male attributes propensities will come to him as he grows up.
measurable_quantities: comb size and colour, crowing and mating behaviour in caponized versus intact cocks, by age at castration
claims.candidate_data: Classic and modern capon studies in poultry science and endocrinology.

claims.label: Boys castrated before puberty keep a high voice; eunuchs never go bald
claims.claim: Men castrated in boyhood never grow the later hair and keep a high-pitched voice, and a eunuch never goes bald.
claims.quote: if you mutilate them in boyhood, the later-growing hair never comes, and the voice never changes but remains high-pitched
measurable_quantities: voice pitch, body hair and baldness in men castrated before puberty
claims.candidate_data: Historical studies of castrati and eunuchs and clinical data on androgen deficiency and androgenetic alopecia.

claims.label: Stags castrated before growing horns never grow them
claims.claim: Stags castrated before they have horns never grow horns, and stags castrated when they have horns keep them unchanged in size and do not shed them.
claims.quote: If stags be mutilated, when, by reason of their age, they have as yet no horns, they never grow horns at all; if they be mutilated when they have horns, the horns remain unchanged in size, and the animal does not lose them.
measurable_quantities: antler growth and casting after castration at different ages
claims.candidate_data: Endocrinological studies of castration and testosterone in the antler cycle of deer.

claims.label: Animals lacking upper teeth are the ones that ruminate
claims.claim: The animals that ruminate are those lacking upper (front) teeth, such as cattle, sheep and goats, though a few with teeth in both jaws also ruminate.
claims.quote: It is the animals that lack the upper teeth that ruminate, such as kine, sheep, and goats.
measurable_quantities: co-occurrence of absent upper incisors and rumination across mammals
claims.candidate_data: Dental formulae from mammal comparative anatomy, Phenoscape, and digestive-physiology classifications of ungulates.

claims.label: Many birds change plumage colour and song with the seasons
claims.claim: Many birds change the colour of their plumage and their song with the season; for example, the blackbird turns yellow instead of black and its song changes.
claims.quote: A considerable number of birds change according to season the colour of their plumage and their note; as, for instance, the owsel becomes yellow instead of black, and its note gets altered
claims.scope: birds generally; blackbird (Turdus merula), thrush, nightingale
measurable_quantities: seasonal moult into different plumage colours
seasonal change in song
claims.candidate_data: Moult and plumage descriptions in Birds of the World and song recordings in xeno-canto.

claims.label: The redbreast and the redstart are one bird in two seasonal forms
claims.claim: The robin (a winter bird) and the redstart (a summer bird) change into one another and differ only in plumage colour; likewise the beccafico and the blackcap.
claims.quote: The erithacus (or redbreast) and the so-called redstart change into one another; the former is a winter bird, the latter a summer one, and the difference between them is practically limited to the coloration of their plumage.
claims.scope: European robin (Erithacus rubecula) and common redstart (Phoenicurus phoenicurus); garden warbler and blackcap
measurable_quantities: species identity of the two forms
seasonal occurrence of each species
claims.candidate_data: Taxonomy in the Open Tree of Life and GBIF occurrence records by month in Greece.

claims.label: Ground birds dust-bathe; waterside birds water-bathe
claims.claim: Birds that do not fly but live on the ground take dust-baths, waterside birds and some straight-taloned birds take water-baths, and most crooked-taloned birds take neither.
claims.quote: Birds that do not fly but keep on the ground take the dust-bath, as for instance the hen, the partridge, the francolin, the crested lark, the pheasant; some of the straight-taloned birds, and such as live on the banks of a river, in marshes, or by the sea, take a water-bath
claims.scope: birds: galliforms and larks; waterside birds; raptors
measurable_quantities: occurrence of dust-bathing and water-bathing by taxon and habitat
claims.candidate_data: Comparative compilations of maintenance behaviour in Birds of the World with habitat data from AVONET.

claims.label: The final cause comes before the motor cause in explaining nature
claims.claim: Of the causes at work in the generation of natural things, the final cause (the end or purpose) is prior to the motor cause, in nature as in art.
claims.quote: Plainly, however, that cause is the first which we call the final one. For this is the Reason, and the Reason forms the starting-point, alike in the works of art and in works of nature.
claims.scope: all works of nature, including animals and their parts
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: The vertebrae are not formed by accidental breaking of the foetal backbone
claims.claim: The division of the backbone into vertebrae is not, as Empedocles held, the result of the backbone being broken by the contorted position of the foetus in the womb, nor are animal characters in general mere incidents of development.
claims.quote: Empedocles, then, was in error when he said that many of the characters presented by animals were merely the results of incidental occurrences during their development; for instance, that the backbone was divided as it is into vertebrae, because it happened to be broken owing to the contorted position of the foetus in the womb.
measurable_quantities: timing of vertebral segmentation relative to foetal posture
presence of vertebral segmentation in embryos before mechanical loading
claims.candidate_data: Embryological staging series and developmental-anatomy ontologies (e.g. Uberon, ZFIN staging for zebrafish) documenting when vertebral segments form.

claims.label: Like begets like: the parent's characters determine the offspring's
claims.claim: Man is generated from man, and it is the possession of certain characters by the parent that determines the development of like characters in the offspring.
claims.quote: For man is generated from man; and thus it is the possession of certain characters by the parent that determines the development of like characters in the child.
claims.scope: all animals that are generated from parents, with man as the example
measurable_quantities: parent–offspring resemblance in traits
claims.candidate_data: Parent–offspring trait regressions and heritability estimates compiled in quantitative-genetics literature and animal-breeding databases.

claims.label: Only man has intellect, though other animals move themselves
claims.claim: Other animals besides man have the power of locomotion, but none but man has intellect.
claims.quote: I say not the intellectual part; for other animals than man have the power of locomotion, but in none but him is there intellect.
claims.scope: all animals, man contrasted with the rest
measurable_quantities: performance of non-human animals on reasoning and problem-solving tasks
claims.candidate_data: Comparative cognition test batteries and published primate and corvid problem-solving studies; no single standard database known.

claims.label: Respiration is driven by an alternation of heat and cooling
claims.claim: Breathing exists for the alternate discharge and re-entry of heat, and the alternation of heating and cooling in the body necessarily produces the alternate intake and discharge of outer air.
claims.quote: For the alternate discharge and re-entrance of heat and the inflow of air are necessary if we are to live. Here we have at once a necessity in the former of the two senses. But the alternation of heat and refrigeration produces of necessity an alternate admission and discharge of the outer air, and this is a necessity of the second kind.
measurable_quantities: temperature of inspired versus expired air
whether ventilation rate tracks body heat or tracks gas-exchange demand
claims.candidate_data: Respiratory physiology measurements of ventilation, expired-air temperature and ventilatory control in mammals.

claims.label: Some ants fly and others do not
claims.claim: Among ants some fly and others do not, so Flying versus Walking cannot be used to divide animal kinds.
claims.quote: For some groups, Ants for instance, fall under both divisions, some ants flying while others do not.
measurable_quantities: presence of winged and wingless individuals within ant species
claims.candidate_data: Ant caste and morphology data in AntWeb and AntWiki, and the Animal Diversity Web.

claims.label: Groups such as Wild and Tame cannot divide species, since tame kinds also occur wild
claims.claim: In almost all kinds of animal of which some members are tame, other members are wild, so wildness and tameness are not specific differences.
claims.quote: For in almost all species in which some members are tame, there are other members that are wild. Such, for example, is the case with Men, Horses, Oxen, Dogs in India, Pigs, Goats, Sheep
claims.scope: domesticated animals: horse, ox, dog, pig, goat, sheep, and man
measurable_quantities: existence of wild or feral populations of the same kind as each domesticated animal
claims.candidate_data: Domestication records and wild-progenitor taxonomy (e.g. GBIF occurrences of wild and feral populations, the Animal Diversity Web).

claims.label: Natural groups are marked by many differentiae, not by dichotomy
claims.claim: Animals should be classified into the natural groups that mankind instinctively recognizes, such as Birds and Fishes, each defined by many differentiae together, and not by successive two-way division on a single character.
claims.quote: The method then that we must adopt is to attempt to recognize the natural groups, following the indications afforded by the instincts of mankind, which led them for instance to form the class of Birds and the class of Fishes, each of which groups combines a multitude of differentiae, and is not defined by a single one as in dichotomy.
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Within a class animals differ by degree; across classes their parts are only analogous
claims.claim: Animals within one class differ only by degree (more and less of the same part), while different classes agree only in having analogous organs, as the bird's feather corresponds to the fish's scale.
claims.quote: For instance, bird differs from bird by gradation, or by excess and defect; some birds have long feathers, others short ones, but all are feathered. Bird and Fish are more remote and only agree in having analogous organs; for what in the bird is feather, in the fish is scale.
claims.scope: birds and fishes as examples of classes
measurable_quantities: correspondence of feathers and fish scales in structure and development
claims.candidate_data: Comparative integument anatomy and homology annotations in Uberon and the Phenoscape Knowledgebase.

claims.label: Groups lacking lungs or blood have analogous organs and fluids in their place
claims.claim: Some groups of animals have lungs and others have instead an organ analogous to a lung; some have blood and others have instead a fluid analogous to blood with the same office.
claims.quote: For instance, some groups have lungs, others have no lung, but an organ analogous to a lung in its place; some have blood, others have no blood, but a fluid analogous to blood, and with the same office.
claims.scope: all animals: lunged versus unlunged, animals with blood versus bloodless animals
measurable_quantities: presence of lungs or other respiratory organs across taxa
presence of a circulating fluid in animals Aristotle calls bloodless
claims.candidate_data: Comparative anatomy in Uberon and the Phenoscape Knowledgebase; the Animal Diversity Web.

claims.label: The body exists for the soul and each part for its function
claims.claim: As each instrument serves some action, the body is made for the soul and each part of the body for some subordinate function to which it is adapted.
claims.quote: Thus the saw is made for sawing, for sawing is a function, and not sawing for the saw. Similarly, the body too must somehow or other be made for the soul, and each part of it for some subordinate function, to which it is adapted.
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Homogeneous tissues exist for the sake of the heterogeneous organs
claims.claim: Animals are composed of homogeneous parts (such as bone and flesh) and heterogeneous parts (such as face and hand), and the homogeneous parts exist for the sake of the heterogeneous ones, which carry on the body's functions.
claims.quote: Animals, then, are composed of homogeneous parts, and are also composed of heterogeneous parts. The former, however, exist for the sake of the latter. For the active functions and operations of the body are carried on by these; that is, by the heterogeneous parts, such as the eye, the nostril, the whole face, the fingers, the hand, and the whole arm.
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: The heart is the seat of sensation, motion and nutrition in blooded animals
claims.claim: The sensory, motor and nutritive faculties are lodged in one central part, which in animals with blood is the heart and in bloodless animals the part that takes the place of a heart.
claims.quote: For this reason it is the heart which in sanguineous animals constitutes this central part, and in bloodless animals it is that which takes the place of a heart.
claims.scope: animals with blood (roughly vertebrates) and bloodless animals
measurable_quantities: effect of heart versus brain lesions on sensation and voluntary movement
claims.candidate_data: Neurophysiology and lesion studies; heart-transplant and artificial-heart patient outcomes in the clinical literature.

claims.label: Thick hot blood gives strength; thin cool blood gives sensation and intelligence
claims.claim: The thicker and hotter an animal's blood, the more it conduces to strength; the thinner and colder, the better suited it is to sensation and intelligence; those with hot, thin and clear blood are best for both courage and intelligence.
claims.quote: As regards the results of such differences, the thicker and the hotter blood is, the more conducive is it to strength, while in proportion to its thinness and its coldness is its suitability for sensation and intelligence.
claims.scope: animals with blood, and by analogy bloodless animals
measurable_quantities: blood viscosity or haematocrit
body temperature
measures of strength and of cognitive performance across species
claims.candidate_data: Comparative haematology (e.g. species reference intervals in veterinary literature), AnAge and body-temperature compilations, comparative cognition studies.

claims.label: Blood solidifies outside the body, yellow bile becomes more fluid
claims.claim: Blood is hot and fluid in the living body but becomes cold and coagulates when separated from it, whereas yellow bile becomes more fluid when separated.
claims.quote: Of the former blood is an example, of the latter bile; for while blood solidifies when thus separated, yellow bile under the same circumstances becomes more fluid.
measurable_quantities: clotting of shed blood
viscosity of bile after removal from the body
claims.candidate_data: Clinical coagulation data and biliary physiology measurements of bile viscosity.

claims.label: Nearly all animals, and all that move about, have a stomach
claims.claim: Animals, with scarcely an exception and conspicuously all those capable of locomotion, have a stomach-sac that serves them as an internal substitute for the earth from which plants draw food.
claims.quote: But animals, with scarcely an exception, and conspicuously all such as are capable of locomotion, are provided with a stomachal sac, which is as it were an internal substitute for the earth.
claims.scope: all animals, especially those that move from place to place
measurable_quantities: presence of a stomach or gut sac across animal taxa
claims.candidate_data: Comparative digestive anatomy in Uberon and the Phenoscape Knowledgebase; the Animal Diversity Web.

claims.label: Blood is the final nutriment and its quantity follows food intake
claims.claim: Blood is the final nutritive material of the body in animals that have it; it diminishes in quantity when no food is taken, increases when much is eaten, and is healthy or unhealthy according to the food.
claims.quote: This explains why the blood diminishes in quantity when no food is taken, and increases when much is consumed, and also why it becomes healthy and unhealthy according as the food is of the one or the other character.
claims.scope: animals with blood; in bloodless animals the analogous fluid
measurable_quantities: blood volume during fasting versus feeding
blood composition in relation to diet
claims.candidate_data: Physiological studies of blood volume and plasma composition under fasting and feeding in humans and laboratory animals.

claims.label: Deer and roe blood has no fibres and never coagulates
claims.claim: The blood of deer and of roe deer contains no fibres and for this reason never coagulates.
claims.quote: There are none, for instance, in the blood of deer and of roes; and for this reason the blood of such animals as these never coagulates.
measurable_quantities: clotting time and fibrinogen concentration in cervid blood
claims.candidate_data: Veterinary haematology reference values for cervids, e.g. Species360 ZIMS physiological reference intervals.

claims.label: Bloodless animals are more timorous, freezing and discharging excretions when frightened
claims.claim: Bloodless animals are, as a general rule, more timorous than animals with blood: when frightened they stay motionless, discharge their excretions and in some cases change colour.
claims.quote: This also explains why bloodless animals are, as a general rule, more timorous than such as have blood, so that they remain motionless, when frightened, and discharge their excretions, and in some instances change colour.
claims.scope: bloodless animals (invertebrates such as cephalopods and insects) compared with animals with blood
measurable_quantities: frequency of freezing, ink or excretion discharge and colour change as fear responses
claims.candidate_data: Behavioural ecology literature on defensive behaviour in cephalopods and arthropods; the Animal Diversity Web.

claims.label: Bull's blood coagulates faster than any other animal's
claims.claim: Bulls and boars have blood exceedingly rich in fibres, and the bull's blood coagulates more rapidly than that of any other animal.
claims.quote: This explains why bulls and boars are so choleric and so passionate. For their blood is exceedingly rich in fibres, and the bull's at any rate coagulates more rapidly than that of any other animal.
claims.scope: bulls (Bos taurus) and boars (Sus scrofa), compared with all other animals
measurable_quantities: clotting time of bovine blood compared with other species
fibrinogen concentration in cattle and pigs
claims.candidate_data: Comparative veterinary coagulation studies and species haematology reference intervals.

claims.label: Horned animals lacking upper front teeth have suet; others have lard
claims.claim: Horned animals without front teeth in the upper jaw have fat in the form of suet, whereas hornless animals with front teeth in both jaws and toed feet have lard, which neither coagulates nor dries into a friable mass.
claims.quote: Thus it is that in those horned animals that have no front teeth in the upper jaw the fat consists of suet.
claims.scope: horned animals without upper incisors (ruminants such as ox, sheep, goat) versus hornless animals with incisors in both jaws (such as pig)
measurable_quantities: melting point and saturation of body fat in ruminants versus non-ruminants
claims.candidate_data: Animal fat composition data in food-composition tables (e.g. USDA FoodData Central) and lipid chemistry literature.

claims.label: Fat animals are less prolific
claims.claim: Fat animals are less prolific than others, because the blood that should form semen is used up in making lard and suet.
claims.quote: For the same reason fat animals are less prolific than others. For that part of the blood which should go to form semen and seed is used up in the production of lard and suet
measurable_quantities: fertility or litter size in relation to body fat within species
claims.candidate_data: Livestock reproduction studies relating body condition to fertility, and human epidemiology of obesity and fertility.

claims.label: The lion's bones have almost no marrow
claims.claim: Animals with strong and solid bones, such as the lion, have hardly any marrow, the lion's being so insignificant that its bones look as though they had none.
claims.quote: There are some animals that can hardly be said to have any marrow. These are those whose bones are strong and solid, as is the case with the lion. For in this animal the marrow is so utterly insignificant that the bones look as though they had none at all.
claims.scope: lion (Panthera leo) and other animals with strong compact bones
measurable_quantities: medullary cavity size and marrow content in lion long bones compared with other mammals
claims.candidate_data: CT scans of carnivore skeletons in MorphoSource and comparative cortical-bone thickness studies.

claims.label: The brain is the coldest part of the body and bloodless in its substance
claims.claim: Of all parts of the body none is as cold as the brain, which is cold to the touch and has no blood in its proper substance.
claims.quote: The coldness of the brain is also manifest enough. For in the first place it is cold even to the touch; and, secondly, of all the fluid parts of the body it is the driest and the one that has the least blood; for in fact it has no blood at all in its proper substance.
measurable_quantities: brain temperature relative to other organs
cerebral blood flow and vascularity
claims.candidate_data: Human and animal brain-temperature measurements and cerebral blood flow data in physiology literature.

claims.label: The brain exists to cool the heat of the heart
claims.claim: Nature has made the brain, a compound of earth and water, as a counterpoise to the heat of the region of the heart, to moderate it.
claims.quote: nature has contrived the brain as a counterpoise to the region of the heart with its contained heat, and has given it to animals to moderate the latter, combining in it the properties of earth and water.
measurable_quantities: contribution of the brain to cooling the blood or heart
brain metabolic heat production
claims.candidate_data: Thermal physiology studies of brain heat production and selective brain cooling in mammals.

claims.label: Every animal with blood has a brain; no bloodless animal has one
claims.claim: Every animal with blood has a brain, whereas no bloodless animal has such an organ, except by analogy, as in the poulp (octopus).
claims.quote: For this reason it is, that every sanguineous animal has a brain; whereas no bloodless creature has such an organ, unless indeed it be, as the Poulp, by analogy.
claims.scope: animals with blood (roughly vertebrates) versus bloodless animals (invertebrates), with the poulp (octopus) as exception
measurable_quantities: presence of a brain or cerebral ganglia across animal taxa
claims.candidate_data: Comparative neuroanatomy in Uberon and the Phenoscape Knowledgebase; invertebrate neuroanatomy literature.

claims.label: The brain causes sleep by chilling the blood rising after food
claims.claim: The brain, or its analogue, is the cause of sleep: by chilling the blood that streams upward after food it produces heaviness in the head and drives the heat downward with the blood.
claims.quote: It is the brain again-or, in animals that have no brain, the part analogous to it-which is the cause of sleep. For either by chilling the blood that streams upwards after food, or by some other similar influences, it produces heaviness in the region in which it lies
measurable_quantities: role of the brain in initiating sleep
post-meal drowsiness and blood flow
claims.candidate_data: Sleep neuroscience literature on brain sleep-regulating circuits and postprandial somnolence.

claims.label: Man has the largest brain for his size, and men larger than women
claims.claim: Of all animals, man has the largest brain in proportion to his size, and the brain is larger in men than in women.
claims.quote: Of all animals, man has the largest brain in proportion to his size; and it is larger in men than in women.
claims.scope: man compared with all other animals; men compared with women
measurable_quantities: brain mass relative to body mass across species
brain mass in men and women, absolute and relative to body size
claims.candidate_data: Comparative brain and body mass compilations (e.g. published mammal and bird brain-size datasets), PanTHERIA body masses, and human neuroimaging cohorts such as the UK Biobank.

claims.label: Only in man does the bregma solidify last
claims.claim: In man the cranial bone called the bregma is the last to become solidified, because evaporation continues through it under the influence of heat; man is the only animal with blood in which this happens.
claims.quote: it is again owing to this superabundance that the cranial bone, which some call the Bregma, is the last to become solidified; so long does evaporation continue to occur through it under the influence of heat. Man is the only sanguineous animal in which this takes place.
claims.scope: man compared with other animals with blood
measurable_quantities: age at closure of the anterior fontanelle in humans and other mammals
claims.candidate_data: Comparative cranial ontogeny studies and skull CT collections in MorphoSource.

claims.label: Man has more skull sutures than any animal, males more than females
claims.claim: Man has more sutures in his skull than any other animal, and the male more than the female, because the larger brain requires more ventilation.
claims.quote: Man, again, has more sutures in his skull than any other animal, and the male more than the female.
claims.scope: man compared with other animals; men compared with women
measurable_quantities: number of cranial sutures by species and by sex
claims.candidate_data: Comparative cranial anatomy and skull CT collections in MorphoSource; Uberon for suture inventories.

claims.label: Crustaceans and testaceans have their hard supporting part outside
claims.claim: In all crustaceans and testaceans the fleshy substance is within and the hard earthy matter is outside, and the shell both holds the soft parts together and keeps in their scanty natural heat.
claims.quote: For in all these animals the fleshy substance is within, and the earthy matter, which holds the soft parts together and keeps them from injury, is on the outside. For the shell not only enables the soft parts to hold together, but also, as the animal is bloodless and so has but little natural warmth, surrounds it
claims.scope: crustaceans (crabs, spiny lobsters) and testaceans (shelled molluscs such as oysters)
measurable_quantities: presence of an exoskeleton or shell
heat retention by shells
claims.candidate_data: Comparative invertebrate anatomy in the Animal Diversity Web and SeaLifeBase; thermal biology studies of shelled invertebrates.

claims.label: Cuttlefish and squid have an internal shell; the octopus has none
claims.claim: Cuttlefishes have an internal hard part (the os sepiae) and calamaries (squids) the gladius, but poulps (octopuses) have no such part because their body-sac is short.
claims.quote: For instance, in the Cuttle-fishes there is what is known as the os sepiae, and in the Calamaries there is the so-called gladius. In the Poulps, on the other hand, there is no such internal part
measurable_quantities: presence of cuttlebone, gladius or internal shell remnant
mantle length
claims.candidate_data: Cephalopod anatomy in SeaLifeBase, the Tree of Life Web Project and the Animal Diversity Web.

claims.label: The belly wall is boneless in all animals
claims.claim: The walls of the belly are in all animals devoid of bones, so as not to hinder its expansion after a meal or the growth of the foetus in females.
claims.quote: The walls of this are in all animals devoid of bones; in order that there may be no hindrance to the expansion which necessarily occurs in this part after a meal, nor, in females, any interference with the growth of the foetus, which is lodged here.
measurable_quantities: presence of bones (e.g. gastralia) in the abdominal wall across vertebrates
claims.candidate_data: Comparative skeletal anatomy in Uberon, the Phenoscape Knowledgebase and MorphoSource specimens.

claims.label: Males' bones are harder than females', carnivores' harder than herbivores'
claims.claim: The bones of males are harder than those of females, and the bones of carnivores that get their food by fighting are harder than those of herbivores.
claims.quote: Thus it is that the bones of males are harder than those of females; and the bones of flesh-eaters, that get their food by fighting, are harder than those of Herbivora.
measurable_quantities: bone mineral density or hardness by sex
bone mineral density in carnivores versus herbivores
claims.candidate_data: Bone densitometry studies in mammals and comparative bone-material-property literature; EltonTraits for diet classification.

claims.label: The lion's bones are so hard they give off sparks when struck
claims.claim: The lion's bones are so hard that when struck they give off sparks, as though they were stones.
claims.quote: Of this the Lion is an example; for so hard are its bones, that, when struck, they give off sparks, as though they were stones.
measurable_quantities: hardness of lion bone
whether bone produces sparks when struck
claims.candidate_data: Bone material-property measurements; none specific to lions known.

claims.label: The dolphin, being viviparous, has bones rather than fish-spines
claims.claim: The dolphin, being viviparous, has bones and not fish-spines.
claims.quote: It may be mentioned also that the Dolphin, in as much as it is viviparous, is provided with bones and not with fish-spines.
measurable_quantities: skeletal tissue type in dolphins
claims.candidate_data: Cetacean skeletal anatomy in MorphoSource and the Animal Diversity Web.

claims.label: Selachians have cartilage instead of fish-spine, for undulating movement
claims.claim: In selachians (cartilaginous fishes) the fish-spines are replaced by cartilage, because their undulating movement requires a pliable rather than brittle supporting framework.
claims.quote: Lastly, in the Selachia, as they are called, the fish-spines are replaced by cartilage. For it is necessary that the movements of these animals shall be of an undulating character; and this again requires the framework that supports the body to be made of a pliable and not of a brittle substance.
measurable_quantities: skeletal tissue type in chondrichthyans
swimming mode of chondrichthyans
claims.candidate_data: FishBase for chondrichthyan taxonomy and swimming mode; Uberon and Phenoscape for skeletal tissue annotations.

claims.label: Neither cartilage nor bone grows again once cut off
claims.claim: Cartilage and bone differ only in degree, and neither cartilage nor bone grows again once cut off.
claims.quote: Cartilage and bone are indeed fundamentally the same thing, the differences between them being merely matters of degree. Thus neither cartilage nor bone, when once cut off, grows again.
measurable_quantities: regrowth of amputated bone or cartilage across taxa
claims.candidate_data: Regeneration literature on limb, fin and antler regrowth in vertebrates.

claims.label: The brain is insensible and not the cause of sensation
claims.claim: The brain cannot be the cause of any sensation, being itself as without feeling as any of the excretions; the sensory centre is the region of the heart.
claims.quote: and, as to the other half of their statement, the brain cannot be the cause of any of the sensations, seeing that it is itself as utterly without feeling as any one of the excretions.
measurable_quantities: pain response to touching brain tissue
effect of brain lesions on sensation
claims.candidate_data: Neurosurgical observations of awake craniotomy and lesion studies in the clinical neuroscience literature.

claims.label: Birds and scaly oviparous quadrupeds have no external ears
claims.claim: Birds have no ears but only the auditory passages, because their skin is hard and they have feathers instead of hair; the same is true of oviparous quadrupeds clad in scaly plates.
claims.quote: In birds, on the other hand, there are no ears, but only the auditory passages. This is because their skin is hard and because they have feathers instead of hairs, so that they have not got the proper material for the formation of ears.
measurable_quantities: presence of an external ear (pinna) across taxa
claims.candidate_data: Comparative anatomy annotations for the pinna in Uberon and the Phenoscape Knowledgebase.

claims.label: The seal has no external ears, only auditory passages
claims.claim: The seal, alone among viviparous quadrupeds, has no ears but only the auditory passages, being a quadruped of stunted formation.
claims.quote: There is also one of the viviparous quadrupeds, namely the seal, that has no ears but only the auditory passages. The explanation of this is that the seal, though a quadruped, is a quadruped of stunted formation.
measurable_quantities: presence of an external ear in seals and other mammals
claims.candidate_data: Pinniped anatomy in the Animal Diversity Web; mammal trait compilations such as PanTHERIA for taxon coverage.

claims.label: Some animals close the eye with the lower lid; birds blink with a membrane
claims.claim: Viviparous animals have two eyelids and use both to close and to blink; oviparous quadrupeds and heavy-bodied birds close the eye with the lower lid only, while birds blink with a membrane issuing from the corner of the eye.
claims.quote: whereas the oviparous quadrupeds, and the heavy-bodied birds as well as some others, use only the lower lid to close the eye; while birds blink by means of a membrane that issues from the canthus.
claims.scope: viviparous animals (mammals), oviparous quadrupeds (reptiles), heavy-bodied birds (e.g. fowl) and birds generally
measurable_quantities: which eyelid closes the eye
presence and use of a nictitating membrane
claims.candidate_data: Comparative ocular anatomy literature on eyelids and nictitating membranes in birds, reptiles and mammals.

claims.label: Birds of prey are sharp-sighted, ground fowl are not
claims.claim: Birds with talons, which search for prey by eye from aloft and soar higher than other birds, are sharp-sighted, while common fowls and similar ground-living birds have no such keenness of vision.
claims.quote: This too explains why birds with talons, that have to search for prey by eye from aloft, and therefore soar to greater heights than other birds, are sharpsighted; while common fowls and the like, that live on the ground and are not made for flight, have no such keenness of vision.
claims.scope: birds with talons (raptors) versus ground fowl (Galliformes)
measurable_quantities: visual acuity in raptors versus galliforms
claims.candidate_data: Published comparative avian visual-acuity measurements; AVONET for ecological traits and lifestyle.

claims.label: Fishes, insects and crustaceans have no eyelids
claims.claim: Fishes, insects and hard-skinned crustaceans have no eyelids; insects and still more crustaceans compensate for their hard eyes by having movable eyes.
claims.quote: Fishes and Insects and the hard-skinned Crustacea present certain differences in their eyes, but so far resemble each other as that none of them have eyelids.
measurable_quantities: presence of eyelids
mobility of the eyes (e.g. stalked eyes)
claims.candidate_data: Comparative eye anatomy in Uberon, FishBase and arthropod morphology literature.

claims.label: All hairy animals have eyelashes; birds and scaly animals lack them, except the ostrich
claims.claim: All animals with hair on the body have eyelashes, while birds and animals with scaly plates, being hairless, have none; the Libyan ostrich is an exception, having eyelashes though a bird.
claims.quote: All animals that have hairs on the body have lashes on the eyelids; but birds and animals with scale-like plates, being hairless, have none. The Libyan ostrich, indeed, forms an exception; for, though a bird, it is furnished with eyelashes.
claims.scope: hairy animals (mammals), birds, scaly animals (reptiles), ostrich (Struthio camelus)
measurable_quantities: presence of eyelashes across taxa
claims.candidate_data: Comparative integument studies of eyelashes in mammals and birds; the Animal Diversity Web.

claims.label: Only man has lashes on both eyelids; no quadruped has a lower eyelash
claims.claim: Of hairy animals, man alone has lashes on both eyelids; no quadruped has a lower eyelash, though some have a few scattered hairs under the lower lid.
claims.quote: Of hairy animals, man alone has lashes on both lids.
measurable_quantities: presence of lower-lid lashes across mammal species
claims.candidate_data: Comparative mammalian eyelash measurements in the published literature; museum specimen photographs.

claims.label: The elephant uses its nostril as a hand
claims.claim: The elephant's proboscis is a nostril which it uses as a hand, conveying food and drink to its mouth and tearing up trees by coiling it round their stems.
claims.quote: For the elephant uses its nostril as a hand; this being the instrument with which it conveys food, fluid and solid alike, to its mouth. With it, too, it tears up trees, coiling it round their stems.
measurable_quantities: use of the trunk in feeding, drinking and uprooting vegetation
claims.candidate_data: Elephant behavioural ecology studies and the Animal Diversity Web.

claims.label: Elephants breathe through the raised trunk when crossing water
claims.claim: Elephants, being both land and swamp animals, have a lengthened nostril which, when they traverse water, they lift above the surface and breathe through, like a diver's breathing instrument.
claims.quote: so also have elephants been furnished by nature with their lengthened nostril; and, whenever they have to traverse the water, they lift this up above the surface and breathe through it.
measurable_quantities: snorkelling with the trunk during swimming
time spent in water
claims.candidate_data: Field observations of elephant swimming behaviour and the Animal Diversity Web.

claims.label: Birds that pronounce letters best have the broadest tongues
claims.claim: Among birds, those most capable of pronouncing letters have the broadest tongues, whereas viviparous quadrupeds, whose tongue is hard, thick and not free, have very limited vocal articulation.
claims.quote: What has been said explains why, among birds, those that are most capable of pronouncing letters are such as have the broadest tongues; and why the viviparous and sanguineous quadrupeds, where the tongue is hard and thick and not free in its motions, have a very limited vocal articulation.
claims.scope: birds (especially talking birds such as parrots) and viviparous quadrupeds (mammals)
measurable_quantities: tongue breadth
capacity for vocal imitation of human speech
claims.candidate_data: Comparative studies of vocal mimicry in parrots and other birds, with tongue morphology from museum specimens; AVONET for taxon coverage.

claims.label: All birds communicate with their tongues, some seeming to teach one another
claims.claim: All birds use their tongues to communicate with each other, some more than others, so that in some cases it seems as though actual instruction passes from one bird to another.
claims.quote: All birds use their tongues to communicate with each other. But some do this in a greater degree than the rest; so that in some cases it even seems as though actual instruction were imparted from one to another by its agency.
measurable_quantities: prevalence of vocal communication across bird species
occurrence of vocal learning from tutors
claims.candidate_data: Song-learning and vocal-learning literature, xeno-canto recordings, and AVONET for taxon coverage.

claims.label: Serpents and lizards have long forked tongues suited to taste
claims.claim: Land-dwelling oviparous animals with blood mostly have a tongue tied down and hard, but in serpents and lizards it is long and forked, suiting it to the perception of savours.
claims.quote: As to those oviparous and sanguineous animals that live not in the air but on the earth, their tongue in most cases is tied down and hard, and is therefore useless for vocal purposes; in the serpents, however, and in the lizards it is long and forked, so as to be suited for the perception of savours.
claims.scope: terrestrial oviparous animals with blood (reptiles, amphibians), especially snakes and lizards
measurable_quantities: tongue length and degree of forking
role of the tongue in chemical sensing
claims.candidate_data: Squamate tongue morphology and chemoreception studies; The Reptile Database for taxon coverage.

claims.label: The crocodile moves its upper jaw and its tongue adheres to the lower
claims.claim: The crocodile's tongue is adherent to the lower jaw, which is immobile; in the crocodile it is the upper jaw that moves, the reverse of other animals.
claims.quote: For the crocodile's tongue is adherent to the lower jaw. For its upper and lower jaws are, as it were, inverted, it being the upper jaw which in other animals is the immovable one.
measurable_quantities: which jaw moves during feeding
attachment of the tongue to the floor of the mouth
claims.candidate_data: Crocodilian skull and jaw-mechanics studies, MorphoSource skull scans and The Reptile Database.

claims.label: Purple snails bore through shells with their tongue
claims.claim: In the purpurae (purple snails) the tongue-like part is so strong that it bores holes through the shells of other shellfish, such as the spiral snails used as bait to catch them.
claims.quote: In the Purpurae, for instance, so strong is this part that it enables them to bore holes through the hard covering of shell-fish, of the spiral snails, for example, that are used as bait to catch them.
claims.scope: purpurae (murex and related purple-dye snails, Muricidae)
measurable_quantities: drilling of prey shells by muricid gastropods
claims.candidate_data: Predatory drill-hole studies in marine gastropods, SeaLifeBase and WoRMS for taxon coverage, and the Paleobiology Database for fossil drill holes.

claims.label: Sharp interlocking teeth and tusks never occur together
claims.claim: No animal that has sharp, interlocking (saw-like) teeth also has tusks; tusks go to animals that strike in fighting and saw-teeth to those that bite.
claims.quote: No animal that has sharp interfitting teeth is at the same time furnished with tusks. For nature never makes anything superfluous or in vain.
claims.scope: mammals with tusks (e.g. swine) and saw-toothed animals (e.g. wild carnivores)
measurable_quantities: co-occurrence of tusks and interlocking carnassial/sectorial dentition across mammal taxa
claims.candidate_data: Comparative dental morphology in MorphoSource specimens and Phenoscape character matrices, with taxa placed on the Open Tree of Life.

claims.label: Nature gives each weapon only, or most fully, to animals that can use it
claims.claim: Nature allots each offensive or defensive weapon (sting, spur, horn, tusk) only, or in a more developed form, to the animals that can use it, and in its most perfect form to those that can use it best.
claims.quote: Nature allots each weapon, offensive and defensive alike, to those animals alone that can use it; or, if not to them alone, to them in a more marked degree; and she allots it in its most perfect state to those that can use it best
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Weapons such as horns and spurs are confined to or larger in males
claims.claim: Because males are stronger and more spirited than females, weapons such as horns, tusks and spurs are found only in males in some species and are more fully developed in males in others (e.g. stags have horns and hinds none; hens often lack the spurs of cocks).
claims.quote: Thus as males are stronger and more choleric than females, it is in males that such parts as those just mentioned are found, either exclusively, as in some species, or more fully developed, as in others.
claims.scope: animals with horns, tusks or spurs: deer, cattle, sheep, spurred birds
measurable_quantities: presence and size of horns, antlers, tusks and spurs in males versus females of each species
claims.candidate_data: Sexual-dimorphism trait data in the Animal Diversity Web and the Amniote Life-History Database, with antler/horn presence by sex from bovid and cervid species accounts.

claims.label: All fishes have saw-like teeth except the parrot-fish (Scarus)
claims.claim: All fishes have sharp, serrated (saw-like) teeth, with the single exception of the Scarus (parrot-fish).
claims.quote: All fishes have teeth of the serrated form, with the single exception of the fish known as the Scarus.
claims.scope: fishes; Scarus (parrot-fish, Sparisoma cretense in the Mediterranean)
measurable_quantities: tooth shape (sharp/conical versus flat/grinding or fused) across fish species
claims.candidate_data: Dentition and diet fields in FishBase, plus fish skull scans in MorphoSource.

claims.label: Hook-clawed birds have hooked beaks and eat no vegetable food
claims.claim: Birds with crooked talons (birds of prey) invariably have a hooked beak, because they are carnivorous and eat no vegetable food at all.
claims.quote: Thus in those birds that are called Crooked-clawed it is invariably hooked, inasmuch as these birds are carnivorous, and eat no kind of vegetable food whatsoever.
measurable_quantities: beak curvature
fraction of plant matter in diet
claims.candidate_data: Beak measurements and trophic niche in AVONET, and diet composition in EltonTraits.

claims.label: True horns occur only in viviparous animals
claims.claim: True horns exist only in viviparous animals; what are called horns in some egg-laying animals are horns only by metaphor and are never used for fighting.
claims.quote: They exist in none but viviparous animals; though in some ovipara certain parts are metaphorically spoken of as horns, in virtue of a certain resemblance.
claims.scope: viviparous animals (mammals) versus egg-laying animals (reptiles, birds, fishes, insects)
measurable_quantities: presence of horn-like head appendages and their use in combat across taxa
claims.candidate_data: Anatomy and behaviour accounts in the Animal Diversity Web and head-appendage characters in Phenoscape.

claims.label: Deer alone have solid horns and alone shed them
claims.claim: Deer are the only animals whose horns are solid throughout, and the only animals that shed their horns.
claims.quote: Deer are the only animals in which the horns are solid throughout, and are also the only animals that cast them.
measurable_quantities: horn/antler structure (solid bone versus keratin sheath over bony core)
annual shedding
claims.candidate_data: Cranial-appendage descriptions for Cervidae, Bovidae, Antilocapridae and Giraffidae in the Animal Diversity Web and Phenoscape.

claims.label: No horned animal has front teeth in the upper jaw
claims.claim: No horned animal has front teeth in both jaws; the upper front teeth are lacking, because the material taken from the teeth is added to the horns.
claims.quote: Thus it is that no animal that has horns has also front teeth in both jaws, those in the upper jaw being deficient. For nature by subtracting from the teeth adds to the horns
claims.scope: horned mammals (bovids, deer and other ruminants)
measurable_quantities: presence of upper incisors in horned versus hornless mammal species
claims.candidate_data: Dental formulae in the Animal Diversity Web and dental characters in Phenoscape, mapped on the Open Tree of Life.

claims.label: Animals without a lung have no neck
claims.claim: An animal that has no lung has no neck, the neck existing for the windpipe; fishes are an example.
claims.quote: Therefore it is that, when there is no lung, there is also no neck. Of this condition the Fishes are an example.
measurable_quantities: presence of a lung
presence of a neck (cervical region) across vertebrate taxa
claims.candidate_data: Cervical-region and lung characters in Uberon and the Phenoscape Knowledgebase.

claims.label: Only hairy, lunged animals have an epiglottis
claims.claim: An epiglottis is found only in animals with blood that have a lung and a hairy skin; animals covered with scaly plates or feathers have none, the larynx itself closing instead.
claims.quote: This part is not found in all sanguineous animals, but only in such of them as have a lung; nor in all of these, but only in such as at the same time have their skin covered with hairs, and not either with scaly plates or with feathers.
claims.scope: animals with blood: hairy viviparous quadrupeds (mammals) versus reptiles and birds
measurable_quantities: presence of an epiglottis across vertebrate classes
claims.candidate_data: Laryngeal anatomy in Uberon and Phenoscape, and comparative anatomy specimens in MorphoSource.

claims.label: Only animals with blood have viscera
claims.claim: Viscera (heart, lung, liver, spleen, kidneys) are found only in animals with blood; no bloodless animal has any viscera at all.
claims.quote: These are peculiar to sanguineous animals, some of which have all of them, others only a part, while no bloodless animals have any at all.
claims.scope: animals with blood (roughly vertebrates) versus bloodless animals (cephalopods, crustaceans, testaceans, insects)
measurable_quantities: presence of heart, liver/digestive gland, kidney-like organs in invertebrate taxa
claims.candidate_data: Invertebrate organ anatomy in Uberon and the Animal Diversity Web.

claims.label: The heart is the first part formed and at once contains blood
claims.claim: In animals with blood the heart is the first of all the parts to be formed in the embryo, and it contains blood as soon as it is formed.
claims.quote: For the heart is the first of all the parts to be formed; and no sooner is it formed than it contains blood.
claims.scope: embryos of animals with blood (e.g. the chick in the egg)
measurable_quantities: order of organ formation in vertebrate embryos
timing of first heartbeat and blood in the heart
claims.candidate_data: Embryonic staging series and developmental-stage ontologies (e.g. Hamburger–Hamilton chick stages, ZFIN zebrafish stages).

claims.label: The heart is the source of all sensation, pain and pleasure
claims.claim: The motions of pain, pleasure and all sensation have their source in the heart and end there; the heart, not the head, is the primary seat of sensation.
claims.quote: Moreover, the motions of pain and pleasure, and generally of all sensation, plainly have their source in the heart, and find in it their ultimate termination.
measurable_quantities: site of sensory integration (heart versus brain) as shown by lesion or recording experiments
claims.candidate_data: Neuroanatomy and lesion literature indexed in Europe PMC; no single dataset.

claims.label: Only in man does the heart lie to the left of centre
claims.claim: In every animal except man the heart lies in the middle of the chest; in man it inclines a little to the left, to counterbalance the coldness of that side.
claims.quote: In all animals but man the heart is placed in the centre of the pectoral region; but in man it inclines a little towards the left, so that it may counterbalance the chilliness of that side.
claims.scope: man versus other animals with blood
measurable_quantities: lateral position of the heart in the thorax across mammals
claims.candidate_data: Thoracic CT and dissection data in MorphoSource and veterinary anatomy references.

claims.label: Only the horse and a kind of ox have a bone in the heart
claims.claim: No animal has a bone in its heart except the horse and a certain kind of ox, where the large heart needs a bony support.
claims.quote: In no animals does the heart contain a bone, certainly in none of those that we have ourselves inspected, with the exception of the horse and a certain kind of ox.
measurable_quantities: presence of a cardiac bone (os cordis) by species
claims.candidate_data: Veterinary anatomy literature on the os cordis indexed in Europe PMC; no dedicated dataset.

claims.label: Large animals' hearts have three cavities, smaller ones two
claims.claim: In animals of great size the heart has three cavities, in smaller animals two, and in every animal at least one.
claims.quote: In animals of great size the heart has three cavities; in smaller animals it has two; and in all has at least one
measurable_quantities: number of heart chambers versus body mass across vertebrates
claims.candidate_data: Cardiac chamber counts from comparative anatomy (Uberon, Phenoscape) combined with body masses from PanTHERIA and AnAge.

claims.label: Animals with a large heart are timid, with a small heart courageous
claims.claim: An animal with a large heart is timid and one with a smaller, moderate heart is more courageous; the hare, deer, mouse, hyena, ass, leopard and marten have large hearts.
claims.quote: So also when the heart is of large size the animal is timorous, while it is more courageous if the organ be smaller and of moderate bulk.
claims.scope: animals with blood; hare, deer, mouse, hyena, ass, leopard, marten
measurable_quantities: relative heart mass (heart mass / body mass)
measures of fearfulness or flight response
claims.candidate_data: Allometric heart-mass compilations in the comparative physiology literature, with behavioural boldness data where available; no single standard dataset.

claims.label: Blood is the material from which the whole body is built
claims.claim: Blood is the material from which every part of the body is made, which is why nature has laid down vessels like irrigation channels throughout the whole body.
claims.quote: Now just after the same fashion has nature laid down channels for the conveyance of the blood throughout the whole body, because this blood is the material out of which the whole fabric is made.
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Breathing serves to cool; fishes are cooled by water and have gills, not a lung
claims.claim: Animals with blood must be cooled from outside, by air or by water; fishes are cooled by water and therefore never have a lung but have gills in its place.
claims.quote: The external cooling agent must be either air or water. In fishes the agent is water. Fishes therefore never have a lung, but have gills in its place
measurable_quantities: role of gills and lungs in heat exchange versus gas exchange
presence of lungs in fishes
claims.candidate_data: Respiratory physiology literature and lung/gill characters in Phenoscape (lungfishes, bichirs).

claims.label: Viviparous animals have large blood-rich lungs, oviparous ones small dry lungs
claims.claim: In viviparous animals the lung is large and full of blood because of their natural heat, while in egg-laying animals (oviparous quadrupeds and birds) it is small, dry and spongy but can expand greatly when inflated.
claims.quote: In the vivipara it is large and rich in blood, because of their natural heat; while in the ovipara it is small and dry but capable of expanding to a vast extent when inflated.
claims.scope: viviparous quadrupeds (mammals) versus lizards, tortoises and birds
measurable_quantities: lung mass and vascularity relative to body mass
lung volume when inflated
claims.candidate_data: Comparative lung morphometry in the respiratory physiology literature (Europe PMC); lung characters in Phenoscape.

claims.label: Heart and liver, and only these, are found in every animal with blood
claims.claim: Every animal with blood has a heart and a liver, and these are the only two viscera invariably present in all of them.
claims.quote: All sanguineous animals, then, need these two parts; and this explains why these two viscera, and these two alone, are invariably found in them all.
measurable_quantities: presence of heart, liver, spleen, kidneys, lung across vertebrate taxa
claims.candidate_data: Organ presence/absence in Uberon and the Phenoscape Knowledgebase across vertebrate clades.

claims.label: Feathered and scaly animals lack a bladder, tortoises excepted
claims.claim: Animals covered with feathers, scales or scaly plates have no urinary bladder, the tortoises being the only exception.
claims.quote: all these animals, owing to the small amount of fluid which they imbibe, and owing also to such residue as there may be being converted into feathers and the like, are invariably without a bladder. The Tortoises, which are comprised among animals with scaly plates, form the only exception
claims.scope: birds, reptiles, fishes; tortoises and turtles
measurable_quantities: presence of a urinary bladder across birds, reptiles and fishes
claims.candidate_data: Urinary-bladder characters in Uberon and Phenoscape across reptiles, birds and fishes.

claims.label: Feathered and scaly animals have no kidneys, tortoises excepted
claims.claim: Kidneys are lacking in all animals clad with feathers, scales or scaly plates, the sea and land tortoises being the only exception; some birds have only flattened kidney-like bodies.
claims.quote: For these also are wanting in all animals that are clad with feathers or with scales or with scale-like plates; the sea and land tortoises forming the only exception.
measurable_quantities: presence of kidneys across birds, reptiles and fishes
claims.candidate_data: Kidney characters in Uberon and Phenoscape across vertebrate clades.

claims.label: The right kidney always lies higher than the left
claims.claim: In all animals that have kidneys, the right kidney is placed higher than the left.
claims.quote: In all animals that have kidneys, that on the right is placed higher than that on the left.
measurable_quantities: craniocaudal position of right versus left kidney by species
claims.candidate_data: Veterinary and human anatomical imaging data (e.g. CT scans in MorphoSource) and comparative anatomy references.

claims.label: Man is the only animal that laughs
claims.claim: Man is the only animal that laughs, and therefore the only animal that is affected by tickling.
claims.quote: That man alone is affected by tickling is due firstly to the delicacy of his skin, and secondly to his being the only animal that laughs.
measurable_quantities: occurrence of laughter-like vocalisations and tickle responses in non-human animals
claims.candidate_data: Behavioural studies of play vocalisations and tickling in apes and rats indexed in Europe PMC; no single dataset.

claims.label: Viviparous animals with front teeth in both jaws have a single stomach
claims.claim: The stomach is single in all viviparous animals with blood that have front teeth in both jaws, such as man, dog, lion, horse, mule, ass and pig.
claims.quote: Thus the stomach is single in all such sanguineous and viviparous animals as have teeth in front of both jaws.
claims.scope: viviparous quadrupeds and man with upper and lower incisors
measurable_quantities: presence of upper incisors
number of stomach chambers
claims.candidate_data: Dental formulae and stomach morphology in the Animal Diversity Web and Phenoscape, mapped on the Open Tree of Life.

claims.label: Horned animals have several stomachs because they lack upper front teeth
claims.claim: Horned animals (sheep, ox, goat, deer and the like) have several stomachs, because they lack front teeth in the upper jaw and the stomachs make up for the imperfect chewing.
claims.quote: A similar multiplicity of stomachs exists also in the horned animals; the reason being that horn-bearing animals have no front teeth in the upper jaw.
claims.scope: horned ruminants: sheep, ox, goat, deer; also the camel
measurable_quantities: number of stomach chambers
presence of upper incisors
presence of horns
claims.candidate_data: Stomach and dental characters in Phenoscape and the Animal Diversity Web across artiodactyls.

claims.label: The parrot-fish alone among fishes ruminates
claims.claim: The Scarus (parrot-fish) apparently ruminates, though no other fish does.
claims.quote: And this is probably the reason why this fish apparently ruminates, though no other fishes do so.
measurable_quantities: regurgitation and re-chewing of food in parrot-fishes
claims.candidate_data: Feeding-biology accounts in FishBase and the literature on the pharyngeal mill of Scaridae.

claims.label: Rennet occurs in all multi-stomached animals and, among others, in the hare
claims.claim: Rennet is found in all animals with a multiple stomach and, among single-stomached animals, in the hare.
claims.quote: What is known as rennet is found in all animals that have a multiple stomach, and in the hare among animals whose stomach is single.
measurable_quantities: presence of milk-clotting enzymes (chymosin activity) in the stomachs of young ruminants and hares
