claims.candidate_data: Enzyme and gene-presence data in UniProt and Ensembl for chymosin orthologues across mammals.

claims.label: Vipers and selachians produce eggs internally and bear live young
claims.claim: Vipers among serpents, like the selachians (cartilaginous fishes) among fishes, first produce eggs internally and then bring forth live young.
claims.quote: For both these and vipers are externally viviparous, but previously produce ova internally.
measurable_quantities: reproductive mode (oviparity, ovoviviparity, viviparity) by species
claims.candidate_data: Reproductive-mode fields in the Reptile Database and FishBase.

claims.label: All fishes have a gall-bladder, mostly attached to the intestine
claims.claim: All fishes have a gall-bladder, and in most of them it is attached to the intestine rather than to the liver.
claims.quote: For all fishes have a gall-bladder; and in most of them it is attached to the intestine
measurable_quantities: presence and attachment site of the gall-bladder across fish species
claims.candidate_data: Gall-bladder characters in Phenoscape and Uberon for fishes.

claims.label: Horse, mule, ass, deer and roe have no gall-bladder
claims.claim: Some animals have no gall-bladder at all, among them the horse, mule, ass, deer and roe; the camel has only small biliary vessels, and the seal and dolphin have none.
claims.quote: For in some animals there is absolutely no gall-bladder at all--in the horse, for instance, the mule, the ass, the deer, and the roe
claims.scope: horse, mule, ass, deer, roe deer, camel, seal, dolphin
measurable_quantities: presence of a gall-bladder by species
claims.candidate_data: Gall-bladder presence across mammals in Phenoscape/Uberon and comparative anatomy literature indexed in Europe PMC.

claims.label: Gall-bladder size in sheep and goats varies by locality
claims.claim: Sheep and goats usually have a gall-bladder, but in some localities (Naxos) it is enormously large and in others (a district of Chalcis in Euboea) it is altogether absent.
claims.quote: For these animals usually have a gall-bladder; but, while in some localities it is so enormously big as to appear a monstrosity, as is the case in Naxos, in others it is altogether wanting
claims.scope: sheep and goats in different localities
measurable_quantities: gall-bladder presence and size in sheep and goat populations by region
claims.candidate_data: Abattoir and veterinary survey data; none known as a public dataset.

claims.label: Animals without a gall-bladder are long-lived
claims.claim: Animals without a gall-bladder, such as deer, solid-hoofed animals, the camel and the dolphin, are long-lived.
claims.quote: For such have no gall-bladder and live long. But besides these there are other animals that have no gall-bladder, though those old writers had not noticed the fact, such as the camel and the dolphin; and these also are, as it happens, long-lived.
claims.scope: mammals with and without a gall-bladder: deer, horse, ass, camel, dolphin
measurable_quantities: maximum lifespan corrected for body mass
presence of a gall-bladder
claims.candidate_data: Maximum lifespan and body mass from AnAge and PanTHERIA, joined to gall-bladder presence from comparative anatomy.

claims.label: All cephalopods have ink, the cuttlefish most
claims.claim: All cephalopods have ink, and the cuttlefish (Sepia) has more of it than any other.
claims.quote: All Cephalopoda alike have this characteristic ink, but chief of all the Sepia, where it is more abundant than in the rest.
measurable_quantities: presence and volume of the ink sac relative to body size by species
claims.candidate_data: Cephalopod anatomy in SeaLifeBase and the cephalopod literature; ink-sac absence in some deep-sea taxa.

claims.label: Crayfish and some crabs have a second set of teeth in the stomach
claims.claim: In the Carabi (spiny lobsters and the like) and some crabs the stomach has a second set of teeth, because the front teeth are not enough to chew the food properly.
claims.quote: and then a stomach, which in the Carabi and some of the Crabs is furnished with a second set of teeth, the anterior teeth being insufficient for adequate mastication.
claims.scope: decapod crustaceans: Carabi (spiny lobsters, crayfish) and crabs
measurable_quantities: presence of a gastric mill with teeth in decapod species
claims.candidate_data: Decapod foregut anatomy in the crustacean literature and specimen scans in MorphoSource.

claims.label: Sea-urchin 'eggs' grow largest at full moon
claims.claim: The so-called eggs of sea-urchins become larger than usual at the time of the full moon, because the nights are then warmer from the moonlight, not because the urchins eat more.
claims.quote: yet they acquire a greater size than usual at the time of full moon; not, as some think, because sea-urchins eat more at that season, but because the nights are then warmer, owing to the moonlight.
measurable_quantities: gonad index across the lunar cycle
night-time temperature across the lunar cycle
claims.candidate_data: Gonad-index time series for echinoids (e.g. Paracentrotus lividus, Diadema setosum) in the marine biology literature.

claims.label: Every sea-urchin has five 'eggs', five teeth and five stomachs
claims.claim: The number of so-called eggs is the same in all sea-urchins and is odd: five, matching their five teeth and five stomach compartments.
claims.quote: The number of the ova is the same in all sea-urchins, and is an odd one. For there are five ova, just as there are also five teeth and five stomachs
measurable_quantities: number of gonads
number of teeth in Aristotle's lantern
number of gut compartments
claims.candidate_data: Echinoid anatomy in the World Register of Marine Species literature links and specimen scans in MorphoSource.

claims.label: Nature passes from lifeless things to animals by unbroken gradation
claims.claim: Nature passes from lifeless things to animals in an unbroken sequence, with living things that are not animals between them, so that neighbouring groups scarcely differ.
claims.quote: For nature passes from lifeless objects to animals in such unbroken sequence, interposing between them beings which live and yet are not animals, that scarcely any difference seems to exist between two neighbouring groups owing to their close proximity.
claims.scope: all living things: plants, sponges, ascidians, animals
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Cicadas live on moisture deposited from the air
claims.claim: Cicadas find enough to live on in the moisture deposited from the air, insects in general being small eaters because of their cold nature.
claims.quote: In no insects is this so conspicuous as in these Cicadae. For they find enough to live on in the moisture which is deposited from the air.
measurable_quantities: food source of adult cicadas (dew versus plant xylem sap)
claims.candidate_data: Feeding-ecology literature on Cicadidae (xylem feeding) indexed in Europe PMC.

claims.label: Very small flying insects have only two wings
claims.claim: Flying insects that are very small have only two wings, as flies do, while larger ones such as bees have four.
claims.quote: When, however, such insects are of very small bulk, their feathers are reduced to two, as is the case with flies.
claims.scope: flying insects: Diptera versus Hymenoptera and others
measurable_quantities: number of functional wings
body size across insect orders
claims.candidate_data: Insect body-size and wing-morphology data from the insect trait literature and GBIF taxon checklists.

claims.label: In crabs and spiny lobsters the right claw is always the larger
claims.claim: In the Carabi (spiny lobsters and crayfish) and in crabs the right claw is invariably the larger and stronger; only in the lobster is it a matter of chance which claw is larger.
claims.quote: In the Carabi and in the Crabs the right claw is invariably the larger and the stronger.
claims.scope: decapod crustaceans with claws: crabs, Carabi; lobsters (Astaci) as the stated exception
measurable_quantities: proportion of individuals with the larger claw on the right, by species
claims.candidate_data: Claw-handedness studies in decapods (e.g. Uca fiddler crabs, Cancer, Homarus) in the crustacean literature.

claims.label: All cephalopods have eight feet, short in cuttlefish and squid, long in octopus
claims.claim: All cephalopods have eight feet, which are short in cuttlefish and squid and longer in the octopus.
claims.quote: Again, though the number of feet is the same in all the Cephalopoda, namely eight, their length varies in different kinds, being short in the Sepias and the Calamaries, but greater in the Poulps.
measurable_quantities: number of arms
arm length relative to mantle length
claims.candidate_data: Morphometric data for cephalopods in SeaLifeBase and the taxonomic literature.

claims.label: Wolves and lions have a neck made of a single bone
claims.claim: In all other animals the neck is flexible and has several vertebrae, but in wolves and lions it consists of a single bone.
claims.quote: In all other animals this neck is flexible and contains several vertebrae; but in wolves and lions it contains only a single bone.
claims.scope: wolves and lions versus other animals with a neck
measurable_quantities: number of cervical vertebrae and their fusion in Canis lupus and Panthera leo
claims.candidate_data: Skeletal specimens and CT scans in MorphoSource; cervical vertebra counts in Phenoscape.

claims.label: Foals are nearly as tall as grown horses, with relatively long legs
claims.claim: In solid- and cloven-hoofed quadrupeds the lower parts are largest in youth, so that foals are scarcely shorter than full-grown horses and can touch their heads with their hind legs, which adults cannot.
claims.quote: Thus it is that colts are scarcely, if at all, below full-grown horses in height; and that while still young they can touch their heads with the hind legs, though this is no longer possible when they are older.
claims.scope: horses and other hoofed quadrupeds; contrasted with human children, whose upper parts are largest
measurable_quantities: leg length relative to adult leg length at birth
withers height of foals versus adults
claims.candidate_data: Equine growth curves in the veterinary literature; ontogenetic allometry studies of ungulates.

claims.label: Man has hands because he is intelligent, not intelligent because he has hands
claims.claim: Man does not owe his superior intelligence to his hands, as Anaxagoras held; he has hands because he is the most intelligent animal, nature giving each organ to the animal that can use it.
claims.quote: we must conclude that man does not owe his superior intelligence to his hands, but his hands to his superior intelligence.
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Wolves, lions, dogs and leopards have five front toes and four hind
claims.claim: Some polydactylous quadrupeds, such as wolves, lions, dogs and leopards, have five digits on each forefoot but only four on each hind foot.
claims.quote: It is this hand-like office of the anterior limbs which explains why in some of the polydactylous quadrupeds, such as wolves, lions, dogs, and leopards, there are actually five digits on each forefoot, though there are only four on each hind one.
measurable_quantities: digit count on fore- and hind feet
claims.candidate_data: Digit counts in Phenoscape and skeletal specimens in MorphoSource.

claims.label: Mammae: two at the thighs in animals with few young, many on the belly in litter-bearers
claims.claim: Animals that bear few young at a time, whether horned or solid-hoofed, have two mammae in the region of the thighs, while litter-bearing or polydactylous animals have numerous teats along the belly or two in the middle of the abdomen.
claims.quote: Thus in such animals as produce but few at a birth, whether horned quadrupeds or those with solid hoofs, the mammae are placed in the region of the thighs, and are two in number, while in such as produce litters, or such as are polydactylous, the dugs are either numerous and placed laterally on the belly, as in swine and dogs
claims.scope: viviparous quadrupeds: horse, ass, camel, deer, ox, goat, swine, dog, lion
measurable_quantities: number and position of teats
litter size
claims.candidate_data: Teat counts and litter size in PanTHERIA, AnAge and the Amniote Life-History Database.

claims.label: All female quadrupeds urinate backwards; only a few males do
claims.claim: All female quadrupeds urinate backwards, while among males only a few do so, such as the lynx, lion, camel and hare; no solid-hoofed quadruped urinates backwards.
claims.quote: All female quadrupeds void their urine backwards, because the position of the parts which this implies is useful to them in the act of copulation. This is the case with only some few males, such as the lynx, the lion, the camel, and the hare.
measurable_quantities: direction of urination by sex and species
claims.candidate_data: Behavioural descriptions in the Animal Diversity Web and the mammalian behaviour literature.

claims.label: Man alone lacks a tail and alone has buttocks
claims.claim: Man has no tail but has buttocks, which no quadruped has; the nourishment that would go to a tail goes to the buttocks and fleshy legs that upright posture requires.
claims.quote: But man is tail-less. He has, however, buttocks, which exist in none of the quadrupeds.
claims.scope: man versus quadrupeds; the ape as intermediate
measurable_quantities: presence of an external tail
relative mass of gluteal muscles
claims.candidate_data: Comparative primate and mammal anatomy in Phenoscape and MorphoSource.

claims.label: Huckle-bones occur mostly in cloven-hoofed animals, never in many-toed ones
claims.claim: No polydactylous quadruped has a huckle-bone (astragalus), solid-hoofed animals as a rule lack one, and most animals that have one are cloven-hoofed.
claims.quote: As to the polydactylous quadrupeds, none of them have huckle-bones. For if they had they would not be polydactylous, but the divisions of the foot would only extend to that amount of its breadth which was covered by the huckle-bone. Thus it is that most of the animals that have huckle-bones are cloven-hoofed.
measurable_quantities: presence and form of the astragalus by foot type
claims.candidate_data: Tarsal characters in Phenoscape and astragalus specimens in MorphoSource.

claims.label: The river crocodile alone among these animals has no tongue
claims.claim: All oviparous quadrupeds and serpents have a tongue in the mouth except the river crocodile, which has only a space where a tongue would be.
claims.quote: and in all, with the single exception of the river crocodile, there is a tongue inside the mouth.
claims.scope: oviparous quadrupeds and serpents; the Nile crocodile
measurable_quantities: presence and mobility of the tongue in crocodilians
claims.candidate_data: Crocodilian oral anatomy in the herpetological literature and specimen scans in MorphoSource.

claims.label: Oviparous quadrupeds have no upper eyelid and close the eye with the lower
claims.claim: Oviparous quadrupeds have no upper eyelid and close the eye with the lower lid, as birds do.
claims.quote: These animals have no upper eyelid, but close the eye with the lower lid In this they resemble birds
claims.scope: oviparous quadrupeds (lizards, tortoises, crocodiles) and birds
measurable_quantities: presence and mobility of upper and lower eyelids
claims.candidate_data: Eyelid characters in Phenoscape and the herpetological anatomy literature.

claims.label: The crocodile moves its upper jaw rather than its lower
claims.claim: In all other animals it is the lower jaw that moves, but in the river crocodile it is the upper jaw.
claims.quote: While in all other animals it is the lower jaw that is movable, in the river crocodile it is exceptionally the upper.
claims.scope: the Nile crocodile versus other animals
measurable_quantities: relative motion of upper and lower jaw (cranial kinesis) during feeding
claims.candidate_data: Crocodilian jaw biomechanics studies and skull scans in MorphoSource.

claims.label: No animal that is not internally viviparous has milk or mammae
claims.claim: No animal that is not internally viviparous has milk or mammae, so birds, fishes, oviparous quadrupeds and serpents have none; in them the nourishment corresponding to milk is formed in the egg.
claims.quote: This absence of milk is not peculiar to these animals, but is common to all such as are not internally viviparous.
measurable_quantities: presence of mammae or milk-like secretions by reproductive mode
claims.candidate_data: Reproductive-mode data in the Amniote Life-History Database and literature on crop milk and monotreme lactation.

claims.label: Long-legged birds have long necks, except web-footed birds
claims.claim: In birds the length of the neck as a rule follows that of the legs, long-legged birds having long necks and short-legged birds short ones, with web-footed birds as the exception.
claims.quote: For long-legged birds have a long neck, short-legged birds a short one, to which rule, however, the web-footed birds form an exception.
measurable_quantities: neck length
leg (tarsus) length
foot webbing
claims.candidate_data: Tarsus length in AVONET, with neck length from skeletal specimens in MorphoSource.

claims.label: Spurs and talons never co-occur in the same bird
claims.claim: No bird has both spurs and talons; spurs belong to heavy ground birds and talons to birds of prey.
claims.quote: Spurs and talons never co-exist in the same bird. For nature never makes anything superfluous
claims.scope: birds: Galliformes and other spurred birds versus raptors
measurable_quantities: presence of tarsal spurs
presence of raptorial talons
claims.candidate_data: Morphological character data in Phenoscape and species accounts in the Animal Diversity Web.

claims.label: All birds have four toes
claims.claim: All birds, web-footed or not, have four toes on each foot, three in front and one behind (the Libyan ostrich set aside).
claims.quote: In all birds alike, whether web-footed or not, the number of toes in each foot is four.
measurable_quantities: number of toes per foot across bird species
claims.candidate_data: Toe-count characters in Phenoscape and foot-type descriptions in the Animal Diversity Web.

claims.label: Only the wryneck has two toes in front and two behind
claims.claim: The wryneck is the only bird whose toes are arranged two in front and two behind; all other birds have three in front and one behind.
claims.quote: The arrangement of the toes is such as has been described in all birds with the exception of the wryneck. Here only two of the toes are in front, the other two behind
measurable_quantities: toe arrangement (anisodactyl, zygodactyl, etc.) across bird species
claims.candidate_data: Foot-type data in Phenoscape and AVONET-linked trait compilations.

claims.label: Fishes have at most four fins
claims.claim: Fishes that are not broad and flat have four fins, two above and two below, and no fish ever has more than four.
claims.quote: Fishes, unless, like the Batos and the Trygon, they are broad and flat, have four fins, two on the upper and two on the under side of the body; and no fish ever has more than these.
claims.scope: fishes (Aristotle's 'fins' here are the paired pectoral and pelvic fins)
measurable_quantities: number of paired fins per species
claims.candidate_data: Fin characters in FishBase and Phenoscape.

claims.label: Selachians lack gill covers because their skeleton is cartilage
claims.claim: In most fishes the gills are covered by opercula, but selachians (cartilaginous fishes) have none, because their skeleton is cartilaginous.
claims.quote: These gills are in most fishes covered by opercula, but in the Selachia, owing to the skeleton being cartilaginous, there are no such coverings.
measurable_quantities: presence of a bony operculum by fish clade
claims.candidate_data: Opercular characters in Phenoscape and FishBase.

claims.label: Selachians and the dolphin have an underslung mouth and turn on the back to feed
claims.claim: In the dolphin and the selachians the mouth is on the underside, so they turn onto their backs to take their food.
claims.quote: while in others, as the dolphin and the Selachia, it is placed on the under surface; so that these fishes turn on the back in order to take their food.
measurable_quantities: mouth position
body roll during prey capture
claims.candidate_data: Feeding-behaviour studies of sharks and dolphins and mouth-position fields in FishBase.

claims.label: No fish and no footless animal has testicles
claims.claim: No fish has testicles, either external or internal, and neither does any footless animal, including the serpents.
claims.quote: No fish has testicles either externally or internally; as indeed have no apodous animals, among which of course are included the serpents.
measurable_quantities: presence of testes in male fishes and snakes

reproductive mode
